Caracterizar qué tipos de plantas dominan cada vía y cómo se relacionan con el éxito de invasión a nivel de especie
Formular y entregar una hipótesis final en lenguaje natural fundamentada en los datos, cumpliendo el contrato de envío

payload.answer:
ANÁLISIS COMPLETO EJECUTADO (script: analysis/urban_invasion_analysis.py; log completo: analysis/results.txt; 103 líneas de salida). Paquetes usados finalmente: pandas 3.0.2, numpy 2.4.4, scipy 1.16.0, statsmodels 0.14.6 (sin herramientas filogenéticas: Bio/ete3/dendropy no disponibles → familia/género como agrupación, según autorizó).

HIPÓTESIS (respuesta en lenguaje natural):
"Urban land use promotes the invasion of introduced plants mainly by filtering which plant types establish: invasion occurrence rises steeply with urbanization (presence of invaders goes from 8.6% of parcels in the lowest urban-cover tercile to 65.2% in the highest at 500 m), but this is largely mediated by habitat type — urban-habitat plots are invaded in 83% of cases vs <7% in forests/scrublands/rock outcrops (habitat is the dominant predictor, LRT chi2=91, p~1e-15). Within invaded plots, urbanization shifts the invading flora's composition: species introduced unintentionally (annual herbs with the broadest invaded niches) increase their share (54%→67% of invaders from low to high urban tercile), while AgriForest introductions almost disappear (8%→2%, p=0.017) and gardening-introduced woody species decline (38%→32%; conditional Poisson IRR for gardening = 0.43, p=0.043). Thus urban land use favors unintentionally introduced, ruderal annual species over deliberately introduced ornamental/agricultural ones; species success overall is best predicted by unintentional pathway (+9.7 invaded plots vs gardening, p=0.009), broader invaded niche breadth (Kruskal-Wallis p=0.047) and longer residence time (log mrt p=0.03), and the modern flora is increasingly gardening-sourced (75% of 1985-2019 introductions vs 17% before 1500), meaning the urban filter acts on an ever-growing ornamental pool."

EVIDENCIA CLAVE (cifras del log):
1. Parcela (n=632; 191 con invasoras): A1 logística 500 m — OR urban_now=10.37 [1.44, 74.48], p=0.020; con habitat ajustado; OR urban_hist=0.02, p=0.005 (colinealidad urban_now–urban_hist r=0.72 → interpretación conjunta cautelosa). Modelo reducido (sin habitat): OR=1.74, p=0.44, pero gradiente crudo de terciles 0.086→0.227→0.652 → el efecto urbano está fuertemente mediado/confundido por el hábitat. Sensibilidad 50 m: no significativo (OR=1.53, p=0.57); 1000 m: OR=4.97, p=0.14 → efecto dependiente de la escala, máximo a 500 m.
2. A2 conteos condicionales (n=191, Poisson HC1): Gardening IRR=0.43 [0.19,0.97], p=0.043; Unintentional IRR=1.06, p=0.87; AgriForest IRR=1.21, p=0.87.
3. A3 composición por terciles de urbanización: Unintentional 54.1%→58.3%→66.7%; Gardening 37.8%→36.6%→31.6%; AgriForest 8.1%→5.1%→1.8%; chi2 global=9.65, p=0.047; par a par AgriForest low vs high p=0.017; Spearman(urban, fracción gardening) rho=-0.106, p=0.14.
4. Especie (n=81): vía × forma de crecimiento chi2=30.9, p=3.2e-6 (Gardening: 20/42 arbustos-árboles; Unintentional: 18/24 anuales). Éxito de invasión (OLS, SE agrupados por familia): Unintentional beta=+9.7, p=0.009; Perennial beta=-3.1, p=0.0001; log(mrt) beta=+2.3, p=0.03; R2=0.23. Nicho invadido mayor en Unintentional (0.75) que Gardening (0.45), KW p=0.047.
5. Temporal (Cataluña): Gardening pasa de 16.8% (antes de 1500) a 75.2% (1985-2019); AgriForest de 51.4% a 6.1%.
6. Diagnósticos: autocorrelación espacial de residuos logísticos despreciable (I≈0.0003, pares aleatorios <5 km); sobredispersión leve solo en n.unint (var 1.97 vs media 1.51); dummies de cambio 1956-2009 con |r|≤0.32 frente a coberturas (sin colinealidad severa; se reportan con cautela como pidió).

LIMITACIONES: (i) sin unión especie-parcela explícita, el efecto sobre "tipos" se infiere vía conteos por vía; (ii) el efecto urbano sobre presencia es dependiente de escala y en gran parte mediado por el hábitat — la afirmación sólida es la del cambio de composición; (iii) n.agfo escaso (23 conteos) limita potencia; (iv) OR del modelo completo con IC muy anchos (variable de cobertura 0-1); (v) filogenia no utilizable en este entorno (solo 77/81 tips emparejados; 4 duplicados con sufijo '2'); se usó familia como agrupación.
payload.evidence: Log completo en analysis/results.txt: secciones SANITY (632 parcelas/37 cols, 0 NAs; 81 especies/19 cols; 77/77 tips del árbol emparejados con 81 etiquetas, 4 duplicados '2' sin pareja), TEMPORAL, SPECIES (chi2=30.93 p=3.17e-06; OLS R2=0.232 con términos significativos listados), colinealidad de dummies, A1 (500m/50m/1000m con OR e IC), A2 (IRR por vía), A3 (tabla de composición por terciles + chi2=9.65 p=0.0468), Moran I=0.0003, tasas de presencia por hábitat (Urban 0.831 vs Bosques 0.044-0.065), composición de hábitat por tercile urbano (Urban: 0%→2.5%→30.3%), y modelos reducidos (OR=1.74 p=0.44 sin ajustar por hábitat).
uncertainties: El efecto urbano sobre la PRESENCIA de invasoras es dependiente de escala (significativo a 500 m, no a 50/1000 m) y está mediado por el hábitat; el hallazgo más robusto es el cambio de COMPOSICIÓN por vía
OR=10.4 con IC [1.4,74] refleja la escala 0-1 de la cobertura; no debe leerse como efecto por punto porcentual
La dirección causal urbano→composición no es demostrable con datos observacionales; la hipótesis es mecanística y plausible, no probada
El efecto negativo de urban_hist (OR=0.02) probablemente refleja supresión por colinealidad (r=0.72) y no un efecto histórico real

payload.hypothesis: Urban land use promotes the invasion of introduced plants mainly by filtering which plant types establish: invasion occurrence rises steeply with urbanization (8.6% of parcels with invaders in the lowest urban-cover tercile vs 65.2% in the highest, 500 m buffer), but this is largely mediated by habitat type (urban-habitat plots 83% invaded vs <7% in forests/scrub; habitat LRT p~1e-15). Within invaded plots, urbanization shifts composition of the invading flora: unintentionally introduced annual herbs with the broadest invaded niches increase their share (54%→67% from low to high urban tercile), while AgriForest introductions decline sharply (8%→2%, p=0.017) and gardening-introduced woody species decline mildly (38%→32%; gardening IRR=0.43, p=0.043). Overall invasion success is higher for unintentionally introduced species (+9.7 invaded plots vs gardening, p=0.009), species with broader invaded niche breadth (p=0.047) and longer residence time (p=0.03); and because the regional introduction pool is increasingly gardening-sourced (17% before 1500 → 75% in 1985-2019), the urban filter increasingly acts on an ornamental-dominated pool, favouring its ruderal, unintentionally-spread component.
payload.workflow: 1) Data inspection and sanity checks (dimensions, NAs, phylo tip matching 77/81, n.total=rowwise sum verified). 2) Plot-level (invaded_niche_pathways.csv, 632 plots): logistic GLM for presence of invaders with urban cover 2009/1956 + cropland 2009 (500 m main; 50 m and 1000 m sensitivity), covariates habitat/elevation/climate/distances; pathway-specific conditional Poisson GLMs (HC1) for n.gard/n.unint/n.agfo given n.total>0; composition of invaders across urbanization terciles with chi-square tests and Spearman trend; Moran-like residual autocorrelation check. 3) Species-level (invasion_success_pathways.csv, 81 species): pathway x growth.form cross-tab (chi-square), OLS of number of invaded plots on pathway x growth.form + log residence time + height with family-clustered SEs (phylogeny tools unavailable in environment), Kruskal-Wallis for niche breadth. 4) Temporal context from contingency table. 5) Supplementary: reduced models without habitat, overdispersion check, collinearity of land-change dummies, Urban-habitat-specific correlation. Tools: pandas 3.0.2, numpy, scipy 1.16.0, statsmodels 0.14.6.
payload.limitations: No explicit species-plot join (link via introduction pathway only); urban effect on occurrence is scale-dependent and largely habitat-mediated (solid claim is the compositional shift); n.agfo sparse (23 counts); wide CIs due to 0-1 cover scale; phylogeny not usable in this environment (family used as grouping; 4 duplicated tip labels unmatched).

- 列名：`introduction.period`、`pathway`、`n`。
- 内容：4 个时期（Before 1500、1501-1900、1901-1984、1985-2019）× 3 条途径（AgriForest、Gardening、Unintentional）的完整列联表，无缺失值。计数示例：Before 1500 的 AgriForest=55 / Gardening=18 / Unintentional=34；1985-2019 的 Gardening 高达 397。可见园艺途径在近代占绝对主导。

**（2）phylogenetic_tree.txt**
- 单行 Newick 格式树，约 3.5 KB，含 81 个 tip 标签（如 `Acer_negundo`、`Pinus_radiata`），根部标注 `Spermatophyta`，带分支长度（遗传/演化距离）。
- **全部 81 个 `invasion_success_pathways.csv` 中的 `phylo.tip.label` 都能精确匹配到树的 tip**（81/81 匹配，无缺失映射）。

**（3）invasion_success_pathways.csv**
- 实际规模：82 行（含表头）× 19 列 → **81 个物种记录**，与文档描述的列完全一致。
- `duplicated` 字段：**确有 4 条 TRUE 记录**（Eucalyptus camaldulensis、Opuntia ficus-indica、Oxalis debilis、Populus deltoides），且这 4 个学名各自在表中重复出现 2 次（同一物种两条记录，其余 77 条为 FALSE）。即存在"同物种多记录"情况，需在物种层面汇总时去重或聚合。
- `intro.pathway` 取值清单：**Gardening 42、Unintentional 30、AgriForest 9**。
- `growth.form` 取值清单：**Perennial fg 30、Shrub/tree 27、Annual fg 24**（三种，无缺失）。
- 缺失值：`genus.relative` 缺 79/81、`species.relative` 缺 77/81（与文档"标记为 NA"的说法一致，这两列实际无信息）；其余 17 列无缺失。
- 其他字段完整：number.of.invaded.plots、area.of.occupancy.10km、habitat.range、invaded.niche.breadth、mrt、native.niche.breadth、dispersal（含 Unspecific/Wind 等）、vegetative（Yes 35 / No 46）、height 均完整。

**（4）invaded_niche_pathways.csv**
- 实际规模：633 行（含表头）× 37 列 → **632 个样方记录**；文档列出的 37 个变量全部存在，无缺失列。

- 各数据集角色：A 提供引入途径的时代背景；B 提供物种性状与入侵成功（并可检验"园艺种更依赖城市"的性状假设）；C 提供样方尺度的因果推断主体（城市覆盖 × 途径交互是核心检验项：**urban × pathway 交互显著且园艺途径斜率更陡 → 城市化主要促进入园艺引入种的入侵**）。

payload.answer:
**最终假设（自然语言，数据为据）**

城市土地利用并不是一个无差别地放大所有外来植物入侵的"总开关"，而是一个**按引入途径区分的过滤器，其作用主要在景观尺度（500–1000 m 缓冲）显现，而非样方级微生境（50 m）**。具体而言：(1) 一个多世纪以来引入途径结构已发生根本转变——园艺途径占新引入种的份额从 1500 年前的 17% 升至 1985–2019 年的 75%（线性趋势 r=+0.97, p=0.031），使园艺种成为当代入侵种库的主体，但园艺种在样方尺度的出现对当前城市覆盖相对不敏感（甚至轻微下降，50m 尺度 IRR=0.70, p=0.21）；(2) 城市覆盖与引入途径存在显著的尺度依赖交互（500m: LR=7.41, p=0.025；1000m: LR=9.31, p=0.0095；50m: p=0.34）——无意引入种（其入侵生态位宽度显著更宽，中位 0.871 vs 园艺种 0.363）随周边城市覆盖增加而增多（1000m 交互 β=+0.73, IRR≈2.1），而农业林业引入种在城市化景观中被强烈排除（500m 交互 β=−1.84, p=0.024；1000m β=−2.45, IRR=0.09, p=0.014；城市覆盖从 0 升至 0.75 时预测计数降至原来的 ~0.2 倍）；(3) 历史 1956–2009 土地利用变化（progressive/regressive）在控制当前覆盖后无独立效应（所有 p>0.7），AIC 支持以"当前城市覆盖"为主解释（1000m 处 M1 AIC=1690.0 vs 变化模型 1699.5），说明当前景观结构而非历史变化轨迹塑造了途径特异的入侵格局。

一句话：**城市化通过"抑制农业林业引入种、促进无意引入种、对园艺种近乎中性"的途径特异过滤重塑入侵植物群落，且该过滤作用随缓冲尺度增大而增强，主要由当前城市覆盖而非 1956–2009 的历史变化驱动。**

**工作流程（简述）**

1. 数据清洗：invasion_success_pathways.csv 中 4 条 duplicated=TRUE 记录（Eucalyptus camaldulensis、Opuntia ficus-indica、Oxalis debilis、Populus deltoides）按学名聚合并对数值性状取均值，81 行 → 77 物种；invaded_niche_pathways.csv 632 样方转长格式（每样方 3 行途径计数，共 1896 行，plot_id 聚类稳健 SE）；land-cover 比例按 0–1 处理。
2. Part A（时间趋势）：4×3 列联表卡方检验 + 途径份额线性趋势。
3. Part B（物种层面）：按途径的 Kruskal–Wallis + 负二项 GLM（入侵样方数 ~ 途径 + mrt + 生境幅度）；PGLS 敏感性分析（自写 Newick 解析 + λ 网格搜索，81 tips 全部匹配，λ̂≈0，与普通模型结论一致，仅一笔带过：谱系校正不改变结论）。
4. Part C（样方层面主检验）：负二项 GLM，count ~ pathway × urban.2009 + 生境 + 海拔 + 气候 + 距路/距河，三个缓冲尺度分别拟合；交互项用 2-df 似然比检验；与"历史变化模型"（progressive/regressive 1956–2009，仅 50m 尺度存在该变量，对三个尺度统一使用）分别建模并按 AIC 比较；urban 与变化项 VIF 1.1–9.1（urban 本身无共线问题）；辅以 offset=log(n.total) 的组成模型（191 个非零样方）和边际预测效应量。

**关键支持证据**

- Part A：χ²=230.4, df=6, p=6.3e-47, Cramér's V=0.332；Gardening 份额 0.168→0.446→0.490→0.752；AgriForest 0.514→0.061（r=−0.98, p=0.023）。
- Part B：入侵样方数/分布面积按途径无显著差异（KW p=0.13/0.12）；入侵生态位宽度途径间边缘显著（H=5.91, p=0.052, ε²=0.053），Unintentional 中位最高；PGLS（λ=0.00）证实 Unintentional 生态位宽度更高（β=+0.299, t=2.43）、入侵样方更多（β=+0.447, t=2.28）。物种层面主要预测因子是生境幅度（β=0.61, z=13.3, p<0.001）而非途径本身。
- Part C（M1，IRR=exp(β)，聚类稳健 SE）：
  - 交互 LRT：50m p=0.339；500m LR=7.41, p=0.0246；1000m LR=9.31, p=0.0095。
  - AgriForest×urban：−0.50 (p=0.45, 50m)、−1.84 (p=0.024, 500m)、−2.45 (IRR=0.09, p=0.014, 1000m)——负向且随尺度增强。
  - Unintentional×urban：+0.29 (p=0.39)、+0.59 (p=0.19)、+0.73 (IRR=2.08, p=0.17, 1000m)——一致正向。
  - Gardening 主效应（参照）：urban.2009.1000m β=−0.89 (p=0.08)。
- AIC：当前覆盖模型在 50m（1699.2 vs 1699.5）与 1000m（1690.0 vs 1699.5）优于历史变化模型；500m 处 M1=1694.2 亦更低。历史变化项在任何尺度均不显著（progressive p=0.71, regressive p=0.78）。
- 组成模型（offset log n.total, 500m）：方向一致（AgriForest×urban β=−2.38；Unintentional×urban β=+0.47）但功效低（p≥0.31）。
- 边际预测（500m，urban 0→0.75）：Gardening ×0.72、Unintentional ×1.13、AgriForest ×0.18。

**局限与标注**：n.agfo 稀疏（仅 21 个非零样方），AgriForest 相关结论均为初步性；交互整体 LRT 在 50m 不显著，尺度格局属方向性一致证据而非定论；两数据集无共享键，物种层与样方层仅做途径层面聚合对照；观察性数据，因果表述为机制性解释。

payload.answer:
**最终假设（自然语言，数据为据）**

城市土地利用并不是一个无差别地放大所有外来植物入侵的"总开关"，而是一个**按引入途径区分的过滤器，其作用主要在景观尺度（500–1000 m 缓冲）显现，而非样方级微生境（50 m）**。具体而言：(1) 一个多世纪以来引入途径结构已发生根本转变——园艺途径占新引入种的份额从 1500 年前的 17% 升至 1985–2019 年的 75%（线性趋势 r=+0.97, p=0.031），使园艺种成为当代入侵种库的主体，但园艺种在样方尺度的出现对当前城市覆盖相对不敏感（甚至轻微下降，50m 尺度 IRR=0.70, p=0.21）；(2) 城市覆盖与引入途径存在显著的尺度依赖交互（500m: LR=7.41, p=0.025；1000m: LR=9.31, p=0.0095；50m: p=0.34）——无意引入种（其入侵生态位宽度显著更宽，中位 0.871 vs 园艺种 0.363）随周边城市覆盖增加而增多（1000m 交互 β=+0.73, IRR≈2.1），而农业林业引入种在城市化景观中被强烈排除（500m 交互 β=−1.84, p=0.024；1000m β=−2.45, IRR=0.09, p=0.014；城市覆盖从 0 升至 0.75 时预测计数降至原来的 ~0.2 倍）；(3) 历史 1956–2009 土地利用变化（progressive/regressive）在控制当前覆盖后无独立效应（所有 p>0.7），AIC 支持以"当前城市覆盖"为主解释（1000m 处 M1 AIC=1690.0 vs 变化模型 1699.5），说明当前景观结构而非历史变化轨迹塑造了途径特异的入侵格局。

一句话：**城市化通过"抑制农业林业引入种、促进无意引入种、对园艺种近乎中性"的途径特异过滤重塑入侵植物群落，且该过滤作用随缓冲尺度增大而增强，主要由当前城市覆盖而非 1956–2009 的历史变化驱动。**

**工作流程（简述）**

1. 数据清洗：invasion_success_pathways.csv 中 4 条 duplicated=TRUE 记录（Eucalyptus camaldulensis、Opuntia ficus-indica、Oxalis debilis、Populus deltoides）按学名聚合并对数值性状取均值，81 行 → 77 物种；invaded_niche_pathways.csv 632 样方转长格式（每样方 3 行途径计数，共 1896 行，plot_id 聚类稳健 SE）；land-cover 比例按 0–1 处理。
2. Part A（时间趋势）：4×3 列联表卡方检验 + 途径份额线性趋势。
3. Part B（物种层面）：按途径的 Kruskal–Wallis + 负二项 GLM（入侵样方数 ~ 途径 + mrt + 生境幅度）；PGLS 敏感性分析（自写 Newick 解析 + λ 网格搜索，81 tips 全部匹配，λ̂≈0，与普通模型结论一致，仅一笔带过：谱系校正不改变结论）。
4. Part C（样方层面主检验）：负二项 GLM，count ~ pathway × urban.2009 + 生境 + 海拔 + 气候 + 距路/距河，三个缓冲尺度分别拟合；交互项用 2-df 似然比检验；与"历史变化模型"（progressive/regressive 1956–2009，仅 50m 尺度存在该变量，对三个尺度统一使用）分别建模并按 AIC 比较；urban 与变化项 VIF 1.1–9.1（urban 本身无共线问题）；辅以 offset=log(n.total) 的组成模型（191 个非零样方）和边际预测效应量。

**关键支持证据**

- Part A：χ²=230.4, df=6, p=6.3e-47, Cramér's V=0.332；Gardening 份额 0.168→0.446→0.490→0.752；AgriForest 0.514→0.061（r=−0.98, p=0.023）。
- Part B：入侵样方数/分布面积按途径无显著差异（KW p=0.13/0.12）；入侵生态位宽度途径间边缘显著（H=5.91, p=0.052, ε²=0.053），Unintentional 中位最高；PGLS（λ=0.00）证实 Unintentional 生态位宽度更高（β=+0.299, t=2.43）、入侵样方更多（β=+0.447, t=2.28）。物种层面主要预测因子是生境幅度（β=0.61, z=13.3, p<0.001）而非途径本身。
- Part C（M1，IRR=exp(β)，聚类稳健 SE）：
  - 交互 LRT：50m p=0.339；500m LR=7.41, p=0.0246；1000m LR=9.31, p=0.0095。
  - AgriForest×urban：−0.50 (p=0.45, 50m)、−1.84 (p=0.024, 500m)、−2.45 (IRR=0.09, p=0.014, 1000m)——负向且随尺度增强。
  - Unintentional×urban：+0.29 (p=0.39)、+0.59 (p=0.19)、+0.73 (IRR=2.08, p=0.17, 1000m)——一致正向。
  - Gardening 主效应（参照）：urban.2009.1000m β=−0.89 (p=0.08)。
- AIC：当前覆盖模型在 50m（1699.2 vs 1699.5）与 1000m（1690.0 vs 1699.5）优于历史变化模型；500m 处 M1=1694.2 亦更低。历史变化项在任何尺度均不显著（progressive p=0.71, regressive p=0.78）。
- 组成模型（offset log n.total, 500m）：方向一致（AgriForest×urban β=−2.38；Unintentional×urban β=+0.47）但功效低（p≥0.31）。
- 边际预测（500m，urban 0→0.75）：Gardening ×0.72、Unintentional ×1.13、AgriForest ×0.18。

**局限与标注**：n.agfo 稀疏（仅 21 个非零样方），AgriForest 相关结论均为初步性；交互整体 LRT 在 50m 不显著，尺度格局属方向性一致证据而非定论；两数据集无共享键，物种层与样方层仅做途径层面聚合对照；观察性数据，因果表述为机制性解释。

payload.answer:
## Data Inspection Report (no main analysis executed)

### 1. File-by-file summary

**data/temporal_trends_contingency_table.csv** — 12 data rows × 3 columns. Columns: `introduction.period` (4 ordered levels: Before 1500, 1501–1900, 1901–1984, 1985–2019), `pathway` (3 levels: AgriForest, Gardening, Unintentional), `n` (integer counts). Total n = 1,046 species introductions. No missing values. ⚠️ Quirk: despite the `.csv` extension, the file is **tab-delimited with quoted fields** — needs `sep='\t'`; a naive comma read collapses everything into one column. Gardening introductions grow across periods (18 → 54 → 142 → 397) while AgriForest declines (55 → 36 → 38 → 32).

**data/invasion_success_pathways.csv** — 81 rows × 19 columns, comma-delimited. No missing values except `genus.relative` (79/81 NA) and `species.relative` (77/81 NA), effectively empty. Species-level data:
- `number.of.invaded.plots`: mean 5.8, median 3, max 53; 23/81 species (28%) have only 1 invaded plot (strong right skew).
- `area.of.occupancy.10km`: mean 4.0, median 2, max 25; 29 species have AOO = 1.
- `habitat.range` 1–7 (mean 2.2); `mrt` 6–250 years (mean 95); `height` 0.04–40 m.
- `intro.pathway`: Gardening 42, Unintentional 30, AgriForest 9 (heavily unbalanced).
- `growth.form`: Perennial fg 30, Shrub/tree 27, Annual fg 24; `dispersal`: Unspecific 42, Animal 21, Wind 18; `vegetative`: No 46, Yes 35; 33 families.
- Mean invaded plots by pathway: Unintentional 9.6 > Gardening 3.9 > AgriForest 2.3.

**data/invaded_niche_pathways.csv** — 632 rows × 37 columns, also **tab-delimited with quoted fields** (same parsing quirk). No missing values. Structure: 632 plots with pathway-specific counts of non-native species plus site descriptors.
- Pathway counts are **heavily zero-inflated**: `n.gard` zeros 515/632 (mean 0.27, max 4); `n.unint` zeros 487/632 (mean 0.46, max 7); `n.agfo` zeros 611/632 (mean 0.04, max 2); `n.total` zeros 441/632 (mean 0.76, max 10). Internally consistent: the three pathway counts sum to `n.total` in all 632 rows.
- `habitat`: 10 levels — Scrublands 106, Croplands 92, Coniferous forests 77, Broad-leaved forests 68, Urban 65, Riparian 61, Rock outcrops 57, Meadows 39, Wetlands 38, Coastal 29.
- Land-cover columns (`cropland.*`/`urban.*` at 50m/500m/1000m buffers for 1956/1993/2009) are all fractions in [0,1] (not percentages despite metadata wording). Urban cover grows 1956→2009 (mean 0.04→0.11 at 50m; 0.04→0.13 at 500m/1000m); cropland declines (0.31→0.17 at 50m; 0.35→0.19 at 500m).
- Change categories (`progressive/regressive/no.changes.*`) are fractional buffer shares summing to ≈1 in 627/632 rows; **5 anomalous rows sum <0.5 (4 sum to exactly 0)**.
- Other predictors: `elevation` 0–2236 m; `distance.stream` 0–2208 m; `distance.road` 0–4720 m; `annual.temperature` 6.4–16.0 °C; `annual.rainfall` 436–1289 mm; `annual.radiation` 14919–15390 kJ/m²/day (relative range ≈3% — effectively uninformative).
- No duplicate rows; all 632 coordinate pairs unique (UTM 368645–481175 E, 4562825–4684875 N).

**data/phylogenetic_tree.txt** — single-line Newick. Contains **exactly 81 tips, all matching the 81 unique `phylo.tip.label` values — no unmatched tips**. The tree additionally carries 20 internal (non-tip) OTT labels (`mrcaott…`, `Spermatophyta`, `Pentapetalae`, `Caryophyllales.rn.d8s.tre`) that a naive regex parser mistakes for tips; careful parsing confirms all 81 species labels resolve. ⚠️ No Biopython/dendropy in the runtime — a small hand-rolled Newick parser (or pip-installed package, if permitted) is needed.

### 2. Duplicates and pathway alignment
- The `duplicated` column flags exactly **4 species**: Eucalyptus camaldulensis, Opuntia ficus-indica, Oxalis debilis, Populus deltoides. Inspection shows these are the **same species recorded under two different introduction pathways** (e.g., E. camaldulensis as AgriForest with tip `…_camaldulensis` and as Gardening with tip `…_camaldulensis2`), with identical trait/plot values but distinct suffixed `phylo.tip.label` values (OpenTree taxonomy duplicates); both suffixed tips exist in the tree.
- Pathway vocabularies align 1:1 across the CSVs: AgriForest ↔ n.agfo, Gardening ↔ n.gard, Unintentional ↔ n.unint. Scopes differ: temporal table = 1,046 Catalonia-wide introductions; invasion_success = 81 Barcelona-province species records; invaded_niche = plot-level counts (632 plots).

### 3. Data-quality issues
1. **Delimiters**: both quoted "csv" files are actually TSV.
2. **Zero inflation**: 441/632 plots have zero non-natives total; 611/632 zero AgriForest → plain Poisson GLMs inadequate.
3. **Collinearity**: elevation vs temperature r = −0.96; temperature vs rainfall r = −0.90; urban vs elevation r ≈ −0.5; urban 500m vs 1000m r = 0.95.
4. `annual.radiation` effectively constant → exclude.
5. 5 anomalous change-category rows (4 sum to 0), including high-invasion plots → exclude from change-based models.
6. AgriForest rare at both species (9/81) and plot (mean 0.04) levels → weak power for that pathway.
7. Descriptive signal already visible: mean n.total by habitat = Urban 2.32, Riparian 1.57, Coastal 1.48, Wetlands 1.37, Croplands 1.17 vs Scrublands 0.05, Rock outcrops 0.02, forests 0.06–0.10 — non-natives concentrate in human-modified/wet habitats.

### 4. Proposed analytical approach

**Question**: How did urban land use affect the invasion of different types (introduction pathways) of introduced plants?

**Response variables:**
- Primary (plot-level, n=632): pathway-stratified counts `n.gard`, `n.unint`, `n.agfo` (and `n.total`) — modeled as (a) presence/absence (logistic) and (b) abundance given presence (negative binomial), i.e., a hurdle decomposition suited to the zero mass.
- Secondary (species-level, n=81): `number.of.invaded.plots` and `area.of.occupancy.10km` (negative-binomial) vs `mrt`, traits, and pathway; test whether pathway × residence time explains invasion success (Gardening dominates recent introductions: 397/528 of 1985–2019).

**Predictors:**
- Urban cover (2009 primary; 1956/1993 for historical contrast) at 500m and 1000m buffers (50m buffer mostly zeros; 500m/1000m correlated r=0.95 → pick one, or compare scales).
- Cropland cover as the agricultural comparator — the key contrast for pathway-specific effects (urban should favor Gardening/Unintentional; cropland AgriForest/Unintentional).
- Change categories (progressive/regressive/no-changes 1956→2009) to test whether land-use *change* rather than *state* drives invasion.
- Covariates: habitat type (10-level factor), elevation or annual temperature (not both, r=−0.96), annual rainfall, distance.road, distance.stream.

**Modeling choices (statsmodels 0.14.6 / pandas 3.0.2 available):**
1. Per-pathway logistic GLM (presence) + negative-binomial GLM (counts | presence) with the covariate set above.
2. Pathway-stratified GLM coefficient comparison (urban/cropland effects across Gardening vs Unintentional vs AgriForest).
3. Species-level negative-binomial GLM: `number.of.invaded.plots` ~ pathway × mrt (+ traits), with genus-level cluster-robust SEs as a crude phylogenetic sensitivity check (full PGLS tooling unavailable).
4. Temporal table: 4×3 trend/chi-square test documenting the Gardening-dominated pathway shift.
5. Diagnostics: VIF, overdispersion checks, habitat-stratified summaries.

### Assumptions (consequential — please confirm/correct)
1. Land-cover columns are proportions 0–1 (metadata says "%"; interpretation is scale-invariant for GLMs).
2. Rows are independent plots at unique coordinates; no explicit spatial random effect (no spatial GLMM library guaranteed) — residual spatial autocorrelation will be acknowledged; a coarse spatial-block sensitivity check is optional.
3. The 4 duplicated rows are multi-pathway records, not errors; species-level models will deduplicate (one row per species) with the choice documented.
4. The 5 anomalous change-category rows will be excluded from models using those variables.
5. "Urban land use" operationalized as urban cover fraction (2009 state + 1956→2009 change); the design is cross-sectional and observational, so effects are correlational.

### Uncertainties
- Expected deliverable depth: I assume a data-grounded natural-language hypothesis backed by an executed analysis (DiscoveryBench full_workflow), not just descriptives.
- Whether `n.*` counts are species richness per plot (assumed yes).
- AgriForest conclusions will be weak due to rarity.
- Full phylogenetic comparative methods unavailable; phylogeny used for verification and genus-level clustering only.

## EXECUTED ANALYSIS — FINAL RESULT

**Hypothesis (natural language):**

Urban land use promotes the invasion of non-native plants in the Barcelona province, but its effect is pathway-specific and operates almost entirely by increasing the probability that a plot is invaded (occupancy), not by increasing how many invaders co-occur where invasions establish. Plots with any urban cover within 500 m have ~5× higher odds of hosting Gardening-introduced invaders (OR = 5.37, p = 0.002; OR = 4.79 with habitat controls, p = 0.007), making ornamental introductions the pathway most tightly coupled to urbanization — consistent with Gardening's rise from 2.9% of introductions before 1500 to 65.0% in 1985–2019 and with urban-habitat plots hosting the highest invader loads (2.32 species/plot). Unintentional (accidental) invaders also respond to urbanization but require high urban intensity (OR = 3.87 for >20% urban cover, p < 0.001) and are equally, indeed more strongly, promoted by cropland cover (OR = 13.3, p < 0.001), tracking both urban and agricultural disturbance corridors. AgriForest invaders show positive but non-significant urban associations (OR = 5.70, p = 0.159) — low power, only 21 invaded plots — and their introduction share has declined historically (34.2% → 19.9%). Conditional on presence, urban cover does not increase invader counts (all count IRRs 0.8–1.1, n.s.), so urbanization changes *where* invasions happen rather than *how many* species pile up locally. At the species level, invasion success (number of plots invaded) is governed by ecological versatility — each additional habitat type in an alien species' range raises expected invaded plots by 88% (IRR = 1.88, p < 0.001) — while pathway identity and residence time contribute nothing (pathway × mrt LRT p = 0.96), indicating that urbanization filters pre-adapted, habitat-generalist species from the introduced pool rather than favoring intrinsically different pathway groups.

---

### (a) Descriptives and temporal trend test
- Temporal 4×3 table (n = 1,046 introductions): χ² = 230.41, df = 6, p = 6.3e-47. Shares by period — Gardening 2.9% → 8.8% → 23.2% → 65.0% (+20.0 pp/period); Unintentional 12.4% → 36.1% (+10.0 pp); AgriForest 34.2% → 19.9% (−4.2 pp).
- Habitat means (species/plot): Urban 2.32 (gard 0.69, unint 1.60, agfo 0.03), Riparian 1.57 (agfo 0.21 — highest), Wetlands 1.37, Coastal 1.48, Croplands 1.17 (unint 0.90 dominant) vs Scrublands 0.05, Rock outcrops 0.02, forests 0.06–0.10.
- Species-level by pathway: Unintentional species invade most plots (mean 9.6) vs Gardening 3.9, AgriForest 2.3; AgriForest species have narrowest habitat range (1.56).

### (b) Per-pathway hurdle GLMs (500 m buffer; logistic presence + NB count|presence; HC1 robust SE)

| Pathway (presences/632) | urban_any OR (p) | urban_hi OR (p) | crop_log OR (p) | count IRR urban (p) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Gardening (117) | **5.37 (0.002)** / 4.79 (0.007) with habitat | 1.77 (0.044) | 3.26 (0.079) | 0.96 (0.877) |
| Unintentional (145) | 2.12 (0.096) | **3.87 (<0.001)** | **13.33 (<0.001)** | 0.90 (0.641) |
| AgriForest (21) — LOW POWER | 5.70 (0.159) | 2.20 (0.146) | 7.54 (0.107) | 0.83 (0.193) |
| Total (191) | **2.63 (0.012)** | **3.86 (<0.001)** | **13.96 (<0.001)** | 1.13 (0.648) |

(no-habitat spec; "with habitat" adds 9 habitat dummies — urban_any remains significant for Gardening: 4.79, p=0.007; attenuated for others, showing habitat type mediates part of the effect.)
- **1000 m comparison**: consistent — urban_hi OR = 4.46 (p<0.001) Unintentional, 3.59 (p<0.001) Total; cropland OR = 9.33 (p=0.002) Total; Gardening cropland OR = 5.53 (p=0.020).
- **Change categories 1956→2009** (627 rows, 5 anomalies excluded): regressive change (decline of urban/cropland) associated with higher presence odds of Unintentional (OR 2.96, p=0.063) and Total invaders (OR 3.69, p=0.024); progressive change marginally raises Gardening counts where present (IRR 1.40, p=0.055). Change signals are weaker and less consistent than land-cover state.

### (c) Species-level NB model (n = 77 species after deduplicating the 4 multi-pathway records; 61 genus clusters)
`number.of.invaded.plots ~ pathway × mrt + habitat.range + log-height + vegetative`, genus-clustered SEs:
- habitat.range IRR = 1.88 (p < 0.001) — the only strong predictor.
- pathway main effects n.s. (Unintentional IRR 0.92 p=0.44; AgriForest IRR 1.12 p=0.66); mrt IRR = 1.00 (p=0.99); pathway × mrt LRT: LR=0.31, df=3, p=0.96.
- Marginal negatives: height IRR 0.90 (p=0.056), vegetative IRR 0.79 (p=0.056).
- Secondary AOO model: same pattern; mrt marginally positive (IRR 1.12, p=0.063).

### (d) Diagnostics
- VIFs all acceptable: urban_any 1.61, urban_hi 1.50, crop_log 1.25, elev_z 5.05, rain_z 4.28, road 1.40, stream 1.02.
- NB Pearson χ²/df 0.10–1.10 → overdispersion controlled by negative binomial.

Loaded the three tables (tab-delimited despite .csv extension) and the Newick tree; verified all 81 phylo.tip.label values match tree tips exactly. Built a 500 m design with binary urban presence (urban_any), high-urban intensity bin (>0.2, n=134 plots vs 190 none / 308 low), log1p cropland, standardized elevation/rainfall, log-distance road/stream, and 10-level habitat. Fitted per-pathway logistic presence GLMs and NB (moment-α) count|presence GLMs with HC1 robust SEs, replicated at 1000 m and for the 1956→2009 change categories. Species-level NB with genus-clustered robust SEs after deduplication. VIF and Pearson-dispersion diagnostics throughout. One methodological correction was made during execution: an initial rank-pruning helper dropped the intercept column, producing invalid negative urban coefficients; this was detected via bivariate checks (Spearman positive vs coefficient negative) and fixed — all reported models retain the intercept.

### Limitations
- Cross-sectional design: urban–invasion associations are correlational; causality cannot be established.
- AgriForest pathway is underpowered (21/632 positive plots) — its estimates are indicative only.
- Plots treated as independent; residual spatial autocorrelation not modeled (no spatial GLMM library); genus-clustered SEs are a coarse phylogenetic sensitivity proxy.
- Urban/cropland cover at 50 m buffer is nearly degenerate (mostly zeros); inferences rest on 500 m/1000 m scales.
- annual.radiation excluded (≈3% relative range, uninformative); elevation and temperature not jointly used (r = −0.96).

payload.answer:
【数据检查结果（第1-3项）与正式分析方案（第4项）】

## 1. 基本结构与完整性
- 文件：data/meta-regression_joined_data_heterogeneity_in_replication_projects.csv，共 86 行（不含表头）× 60 列，无全重复行。
- 关键列完整性与类型（缺失值计数均为 0）：
  - project.x（str）、project.y（str）：完整，且互相一致——project.x="Psychology" (68) 对应 project.y="rpp"；"Experimental Economics" (18) 对应 "ee"。
  - discipline（str）：完整，无缺失。
  - ro、rr、fiso、fisr、relative_es（float64）：全部完整，0 缺失。
  - replicated、no、nr、n.r（int64）：完整，0 缺失（nr 与 n.r 均为复制样本量，取值一致，属冗余列）。
- 注意：lab_id 和 aggregated 两列整列为 NA（86/86 缺失），因此不存在多条 lab 记录或聚合标记的问题——每个 study 恰好一行（86 个 study 标识符互不相同），无需做 lab 层面去重或加权处理。

## 2. 分布与重复情况
- discipline：Cognitive 34、Social 34、Economics 18。
- project.y：rpp 68（全部为 Cognitive+Social 的心理学复制项目）、ee 18（全部为 Economics）。即领域与项目一一对应，discipline 的组间比较同时等价于项目间比较——这是需要明确的混淆点。
- 无完全重复行；study 唯一，无"同一原始研究多个复制实验室"的多行情况（lab_id 全空佐证了这一点）。

## 3. 初步描述统计
按 discipline 的原始效应量 ro 与复制效应量 rr（相关尺度），以及 relative_es：
| discipline | ro 均值/中位数 | rr 均值/中位数 | relative_es 均值/中位数 | |rr|<|ro| 比例 | 复制成功率 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cognitive | 0.533 / 0.561 | 0.285 / 0.269 | 0.509 / 0.650 | 82.4% (28/34) | 47.1% |
| Economics | 0.474 / 0.419 | 0.278 / 0.308 | 0.657 / 0.698 | 83.3% (15/18) | 61.1% |
| Social | 0.346 / 0.348 | 0.123 / 0.041 | 0.278 / 0.131 | 88.2% (30/34) | 20.6% |

- 三个领域的复制效应量均值/中位数都低于原始效应量，"缩小"是普遍现象：Fisher-z 差 (fisr−fiso) 总体均值 −0.262、中位数 −0.229（Cognitive −0.289、Economics −0.266、Social −0.233，绝对缩小幅度接近）。
- 差异主要体现在相对缩小幅度上：Social 领域 relative_es 中位数仅 0.13（复制效应量中位数 0.041，接近归零且 18 条 rr 为负值），Cognitive 与 Economics 的相对保留比例更高（中位数约 0.65–0.70）。
- 这只是描述性对比，Social 领域原始效应量本身也偏小（0.35），相对缩小可能部分是回归效应/低先验效应量所致。

## 4. 拟采用的分析方案（待确认）

**主分析（逐对比较）**：
- 对每个 study 计算逐对差 d = fisr − fiso（Fisher-z 尺度，主指标；对 ro/rr 相关尺度做稳健性核对），按 discipline 分组报告均值、中位数、95% 置信区间与配对符号检验/配对 t 检验，并做组间两两比较（Social vs Cognitive、Social vs Economics 等，必要时以 Welch/置换检验或 Kruskal-Wallis 检验 discipline 间差异）。
- 同时报告三种互补结果：(a) fisr−fiso 的绝对差异；(b) relative_es 的分布与组间比较；(c) 复制成功率 replicated 的比例差异（卡方/Fisher 检验）。三者结合才能回答"效应量是否系统性更小"而不仅是"是否显著"。

**关键假设与不确定之处（列出供确认）**：
1. **尺度选择**：以 Fisher-z (fiso/fisr) 为主指标——它经过方差稳定变换，适合比较差异；correlation 尺度 (ro/rr) 作次要核对。
2. **独立性与加权**：每行一个 study，无重复；ro 与 rr 方差不等，可用 se_fiso、se_fisr 做逆方差加权或随机效应 meta 回归（fisr ~ discipline + fiso）作为稳健性分析，默认先报告不加权的配对比较（结果可能对加权方式不敏感，86 条样本下 meta 回归仅作补充）。
3. **方向符号问题**：relative_es 可为负（18 条 rr 与 ro 方向相反，最小值 −0.897），rr<ro 的"缩小"判断需区分 |rr|<|ro|（幅度缩小）与符号翻转；方案中用绝对差 fisr−fiso 和带符号的 relative_es 分别处理。
4. **缺失值**：关键列无缺失，pm_belief、endprice 等仅部分项目有数据，不影响主分析；异常值不删除，但会报告相对_es 的极值并给出含/不含极端值的稳健性结果（如修剪均值或秩检验）。
5. **混淆点**：discipline 与 replication project 完全绑定（Social/Cognitive 仅来自 RPP，Economics 仅来自 EERP），且复制设计（样本量、国家、被试类型等）不同，因此"领域间差异"无法与"项目设计差异"分离——结论措辞需限定为"领域/项目层面存在效应量缩小的差异趋势"，避免因果表述（如"Economics 复制导致更小偏差"）。
6. **措辞**：所有结论以描述性/关联性语言表达（"在 X 领域，复制效应量相对原始效应量平均缩小约 …"），显著性检验仅作为支持证据，不做因果推断；样本量小（每域 18–34 条），置信区间较宽。
7. **可能需要确认的一点**：若研究者希望同时控制 fiso 本身（低效应量研究相对缩小更明显），可在 meta 回归中纳入 fiso 作为协变量。

以上为计划，待确认后我再执行正式分析并产出最终自然语言假设。

## 正式分析结果（按已批准方案执行，脚本：analysis/effect_size_replication_by_discipline.py）

### 1. 各领域 d = fisr − fiso（Fisher-z 尺度逐对差异）的配对结果
| discipline | n | mean d | median d | 95% CI | 配对 t p | Wilcoxon p |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cognitive | 34 | −0.289 | −0.249 | [−0.415, −0.164] | <0.001 | <0.001 |
| Economics | 18 | −0.266 | −0.143 | [−0.447, −0.084] | 0.007 | 0.001 |
| Social | 34 | −0.233 | −0.232 | [−0.304, −0.162] | <0.001 | <0.001 |

三个领域的复制效应量都系统性地低于原始效应量（d 均为负且 95% CI 不含 0）。总体 d 均值 −0.262、中位数 −0.229；仅 13/86 项研究的复制效应量大于原始效应量。相关尺度稳健性核对结论一致（ro 中位数 0.56/0.42/0.35 vs rr 中位数 0.27/0.31/0.04，Cognitive/Economics/Social）。

**领域间差异（d 的绝对缩小幅度）不显著**：Kruskal-Wallis H=1.248, p=0.536；ANOVA F=0.284, p=0.753；两两 Mann-Whitney 均 p>0.26。即从绝对差看，三领域缩小幅度相近。

### 2. relative_es 与复制成功率的组间比较

**HYPOTHESIS (answer to the question):**

Effect size estimates tend to be larger in the original studies than in their replications in **all three disciplines — Social psychology, Cognitive psychology, and Experimental Economics — but the tendency is strongest in Social psychology**. Across the 86 original–replication pairs, the original effect exceeds the replication effect in ~85% of studies overall. By domain, the per-study "original > replication" share is Social 88% (30/34), Economics 83% (15/18), Cognitive 82% (28/34) — so by that count Social psychology shows the most pervasive attenuation, and it is also clearly the domain with the *largest magnitude* of shrinkage: its mean relative effect size (replication/original) is only 0.28 (median 0.13), versus 0.51 (median 0.65) in Cognitive psychology and 0.66 (median 0.70) in Experimental Economics. Social psychology additionally has the most sign reversals (10/34 replications flipped direction vs. 5/34 Cognitive and 3/18 Economics) and by far the lowest replication rate (21% vs. 47% and 61%). A formal test of the magnitude of attenuation across domains (Kruskal–Wallis on relative_es, H=8.34, p=0.016; Social vs. rest Mann–Whitney p=0.002) confirms Social psychology as the domain where original effect estimates most overstate replication effects, while the raw Fisher-z difference magnitudes are statistically similar across domains (Kruskal–Wallis p=0.54). In short: **every domain's original studies tend to overstate effects, with Social psychology the most affected domain and Experimental Economics the least.**

---

**SUPPORTING EVIDENCE**

Primary analysis — per-study paired differences on the Fisher-z scale (fiso − fisr):

| domain | n | orig > repl n (%) | mean dz | median dz | paired t p | Wilcoxon p | sign flips | attenuated (0<rel<1) | rel>1 | mean rel_es | median rel_es | replicated % |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Social | 34 | 30 (88.2%) | 0.233 | 0.232 | 4e-07 | 1e-06 | 10 | 19 | 4 | 0.278 | 0.131 | 20.6% |
| Cognitive | 34 | 28 (82.4%) | 0.289 | 0.249 | 4.5e-05 | 6e-06 | 5 | 23 | 6 | 0.509 | 0.650 | 47.1% |
| Economics | 18 | 15 (83.3%) | 0.266 | 0.143 | 0.0067 | 0.0008 | 3 | 12 | 3 | 0.657 | 0.698 | 61.1% |
| **Overall** | **86** | **73 (84.9%)** | **0.262** | — | **7e-12** | **1.4e-11** | **18** | **54** | **13** | **0.449** | **0.427** | **39.5%** |

- Secondary lens (project): Psychology/rpp n=68 — 85.3% orig>repl, mean dz 0.261, 15 flips; Experimental Economics/ee n=18 — 83.3%, mean dz 0.266, 3 flips.
- Robustness: on the raw correlation scale (ro − rr) the per-domain proportions are identical (82.4/83.3/88.2%) and the sign of the difference agrees with the Fisher-z sign in 86/86 studies — scale choice does not affect conclusions.
- Sign-flip composition: of the 73 studies where the original is larger, 18 are qualitative sign reversals (rr < 0) and 55 are pure attenuation; all 18 flips are also non-replications (replicated = 0), a coherent pattern rather than data errors. Flip rates do not differ significantly across disciplines (chi-square p = 0.29).

Supplementary (labeled) — inverse-variance weighted pooled Fisher-z difference per domain (weights = 1/(se_fiso² + se_fisr²)):

| domain | pooled dz | SE | z | p |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Social | 0.208 | 0.024 | 8.62 | <0.001 |
| Cognitive | 0.206 | 0.038 | 5.48 | <0.001 |
| Economics | 0.013 | 0.033 | 0.40 | 0.69 |

The pooled view sharpens the contrast: Social and Cognitive psychology show statistically robust pooled attenuation of original vs. replication effects, whereas in Experimental Economics the weighted pooled difference is essentially zero — consistent with the ee project powering replications off the original effect size (mean relative_es 0.66, 61% replication rate), so per-study attenuation exists (83% of pairs) but does not survive precision-weighting.

**Workflow executed:** loaded the joined dataset (86 rows, no missing key fields); computed paired differences on Fisher-z and raw-r scales; per-discipline and per-project summaries of the proportion original > replication, mean/median differences with paired t and Wilcoxon tests; relative_es distribution statistics; sign-flip and attenuation counts; chi-square test of flip rates across disciplines; Kruskal–Wallis and Mann–Whitney tests of attenuation magnitude across domains; supplementary inverse-variance pooled comparison. Results saved to analysis/results_by_discipline.csv and analysis/results_by_project.csv.

**Assumptions & limitations:**
1. Domain = `discipline` column; this is confounded with replication project (Economics = ee only; Cognitive/Social = rpp only), so domain and project effects cannot be separated.
2. Per-study comparison of recorded estimates (not a full meta-regression); the pooled weighted comparison is supplementary and sensitive to within-domain heterogeneity.
3. Negative rr / relative_es treated as genuine sign reversals (they count toward "original larger"); relative_es is a signed ratio.
4. Mean dz magnitudes are similar across disciplines (Kruskal–Wallis p = 0.54); the strongest cross-domain claim rests on relative_es (attenuation magnitude) and flip/replication rates, which favor Social psychology as the most affected domain.
5. Economics has the smallest n (18), so its per-domain estimates are less precise; its pooled result (dz ≈ 0) is notable but based on a single, well-powered replication project.

File A (main file): meta-regression_study_data_heterogeneity_in_replication_projects.csv
- 927 data rows, 57 columns, 141 unique "id" values (id = unique O/R pair).
- Row structure is NOT uniformly one-row-per-O/R-pair: 115 ids have 1 row, 10 ids have 22 rows, 16 ids have 37 rows. The multi-row ids belong to Many Labs projects (one row per replication lab; lab_id has 49 distinct values, NaN for 141 rows). seniority.r is constant within every id (141/141 ids have exactly 1 distinct value), but "replicated" varies within 18 ids (because replication outcome differs by lab).
- The rpp ("Psychology") subset: 97 rows, 97 unique ids — exactly one row per O/R pair; lab_id and aggregated are NaN for all 97 rpp rows (so no lab-level duplication issue for rpp). drop==True for 7 rpp rows (rpp.154, rpp.46, rpp.59, rpp.69, rpp.73, rpp.77, rpp.82); these include 3 replicated=1 rows. - project values (full file): ml1=592, ml3=220, rpp=97, ee=18; no missing.
- replicated (full file): 0=517, 1=383, NaN=27. Within rpp: 0=62, 1=35, no NaN.
- seniority.r (full file): Professor=849, Associate Professor=24, Assistant Professor=23, Researcher=16, Assistant=15; ZERO missing anywhere (also zero missing in rpp). Categories observed: {Professor, Associate Professor, Assistant Professor, Researcher, Assistant}.
- seniority.o (full file): Professor=830, Associate Professor=53, Assistant=37, Researcher=5, Assistant Professor=2; zero missing. In rpp: Professor=83, Associate Professor=9, Researcher=5 (no Assistant Professor/Assistant).
- Note: the datasets.json description for seniority.r says "Most senior author in the original paper" — this is almost certainly a copy-paste typo; given the .r suffix convention stated in the dataset description ("Original & replication specific columns may be appended by o & r"), seniority.r is the most senior author of the REPLICATION team. I will treat seniority.r as the intended variable (seniority of the replication study's authors), but flag the .o alternative (see assumptions).

File B: meta-regression_replication_success_data_heterogeneity_in_replication_projects.csv — 143 rows; columns are effect sizes/SEs/p-values/sample sizes only (study, project, ro/rr, fiso/fisr, se, po/pr, po1/pr1, pm_belief, nr, no). It contains NO author/seniority information, so it is NOT relevant to this question. (Its "project" labels are spelled out, e.g., "Psychology", but seniority simply doesn't exist there.)

  replicated=1: Assistant 6, Assistant Professor 10, Associate Professor 7, Professor 8, Researcher 4 (total 35)

(c) Compute the proportion of junior professors among replicated rpp studies: numerator = count of replicated==1 & rpp rows whose seniority.r is in the "junior" set; denominator = total rpp rows with replicated==1. Senior set: {"Professor", "Associate Professor"}.

Гипотеза (для сабмита): «Наиболее вероятный ответ — домен Social (социальная психология): это единственная дисциплина в данных, где студенты являются модальной категорией субъектов и в оригиналах, и в репликациях, и чьи доли students ближе всего к указанным в вопросе 82.4% (оригиналы) и 80.9% (репликации) — в данных 83.8% (62/74) оригиналов и 81.1% (60/74) репликаций в Social использовали студентов. Вывод устойчив к выбору единицы анализа (пара vs сырые лабораторные строки vs мажоритарность по лабам) и к исключению пары с пропусками; Economics (94.4%/100%) и Cognitive (75.5%/81.6%) существенно дальше от целевых долей по исходной (.o) компоненте».

Workflow: (1) загрузка файла meta-regression_study_data_...csv (927 строк × 57 колонок); (2) дедупликация до одной строки на уникальную пару O/R (id): для ml1/ml3 — строка с aggregated=True (ровно по одной на id, проверено: 26/26; subjects.r в ней совпадает с мажоритарным значением по лабам), для rpp/ee — одиночная строка; итог 141 пара; (3) расчёт долей subjects=='students' по .o и .r внутри каждого discipline + проверка модальности students в обеих колонках; (4) выбор кандидата по утверждённому правилу (минимум |o−82.4|+|r−80.9| среди дисциплин с модальностью students в .o и .r); (5) сенситивности: сырые лабораторные строки (927), мажоритарность subjects.r по лабам, исключение пары с NA, исключение drop=True.

Итоговая таблица (основной анализ, n=141 пар, drop-строки сохранены):
| discipline | n пар | students.o | students.r | модальность students (o/r) | расстояние до 82.4/80.9 |
| Social | 74 | 62 = 83.8% | 60 = 81.1% | да/да | 0.016 |
| Cognitive | 49 | 37 = 75.5% | 40 = 81.6% | да/да | 0.076 |
| Economics | 18 | 17 = 94.4% | 18 = 100% | да/да | 0.311 |
Кандидат: Social.

Чувствительность: сырые строки — Social 82.0/78.4 (кандидат Social, расстояние 0.028); мажоритарность по лабам — идентично основному (Social); исключение NA-пары — Social 84.9/82.2 (кандидат Social). Единственный вариант, меняющий кандидата — исключение drop=True строк (131 id): Social становится 93.8/85.9, и по правилу минимизации расстояния побеждает Cognitive (75.5/81.6, 0.076 против 0.164) — по договорённости этот вариант не основной, но отмечаю как оговорку. Стратификация по project (контекст, не ответ): ee 94.4/100, ml1 75.0/100, ml3 90.0/100, rpp 80.4/76.3.

Ограничения: точную пару 82.4/80.9 не удаётся воспроизвести ни одной агрегацией (ближайшие: 82.3% overall-.o и 81.1% Social-.r) — проценты, видимо, из исходной публикации с иным дедупликацией; вывод опирается на правило «ближайшие доли при модальности students», утверждённое исследователем.

INSPECTION RESULTS (executed in workspace, data/):

1) File sizes and rows
- meta-regression_study_data_...csv: 927 data rows (928 lines incl. header). By project: ml1=592, ml3=220, rpp=97, ee=18. Unique pair ids: 141 (ee=18, ml1=16, ml3=10, rpp=97 ids). Rows per id: median 1, max 37 (lab-level replications via lab_id; 49 distinct labs; lab_id missing on 141 rows = rpp/ee/aggregated rows). Column 'aggregated': False=786, True=26 (ml1 16 + ml3 10; one aggregated row per id for those pairs), NaN=115.
- meta-regression_replication_success_data_...csv: 143 data rows. Projects: Psychology=73, Experimental Philosophy=31, Social Sciences=21, Experimental Economics=18. Columns: study, project, effect sizes/SEs (ro, rr, fiso, fisr, ...), po/pr/po1/pr1, pm_belief, nr, no. It has NO subjects.*, NO discipline columns -> cannot answer the question directly; only relevant as cross-context.

2) Missingness and dtypes (relevant columns, study file)
- subjects.o: dtype object; missing 1/927 (row rpp.154, drop=True).
- subjects.r: dtype object; missing 1/927 (same row).
- discipline: 0 missing; values Social (667 rows / 74 ids), Cognitive (241 / 49), Economics (18 / 18).
- project: 0 missing.

3) Distribution of subjects (counts and % students)
- All rows (n=926 non-missing): subjects.o = students 737 (79.5%), anyone 143, community 46, NaN 1. subjects.r = students 744 (80.3%), online 148, community 25, anyone 9, NaN 1. Note: 'online' appears only in subjects.r, never in subjects.o, despite the data dictionary listing it for both.
- Per discipline, row level: Cognitive o 172/241 = 71.4%, r 202/241 = 83.8%; Economics o 17/18 = 94.4%, r 18/18 = 100%; Social o 548/667 = 82.2%, r 524/667 = 78.6%.
- Per discipline, unique-pair level (141 ids): Cognitive o 37/49 = 75.5%, r 40/49 = 81.6%; Economics o 17/18 = 94.4%, r 18/18 = 100%; Social o 62/74 = 83.8%, r 60/74 = 81.1%.

Coherence with the quoted figures (82.4% o / 80.9% r): No simple cut reproduces them exactly. Best matches: Social at unique-pair level gives r = 81.1% (vs 80.9%) and o = 83.8% (vs 82.4%); overall row level gives o = 79.5%, r = 80.3%. Variants tried: drop==False, aggregated!=True, sample-size weighting, same_subjects==1, joint both-students — none yields 82.4/80.9 exactly, so the quoted numbers likely come from the source paper's own sample definition (possibly slightly different exclusions) rather than a plain computation on this CSV. The qualitative signal is nevertheless consistent: Social is the only large domain where BOTH original (~82–84%) and replication (~78–81%) studies predominantly used students; Cognitive has lower original share (71–76%), and Economics is nearly 100% students but has only 18 pairs.

4) Preprocessing considerations (context note)
- Structure: one row per (pair id x lab) for ml1/ml3 lab replications, plus aggregated rows (aggregated==True) and one-row-per-id for rpp/ee.
- subjects.o is constant within every one of the 141 ids (0 ids with >1 distinct value); subjects.r varies within 16 ids (some labs used different subject types); discipline constant within every id.
- Proposed treatment: main analysis at pair level -> for each id keep the aggregated row when present (26 ids), else the first row; subjects.o is unaffected by this choice. Report a row-level (lab-weighted) sensitivity analysis because subjects.r varies in 16 ml1/ml3 pairs. Exclude/handle rpp.154 (both subjects missing, drop=True) explicitly; 10 ids are entirely drop==True (they are ml1 lab rows flagged for exclusion; at pair level I would keep the pair since the pair itself is not invalid, and run a sensitivity excluding them).

5) Proposed approach for the final answer
- Step 1: deduplicate to 141 pair rows (aggregated row preferred), with row-level sensitivity.
- Step 2: compute % subjects.o=='students' and % subjects.r=='students' per discipline (counts, shares, CIs optional).
- Step 3: identify the domain whose shares align with the quoted 82.4%/80.9% and state the natural-language hypothesis: Social (social psychology) is the domain where both originals and replications predominantly used student subjects; report full three-discipline table as supporting evidence.
- Do not use the second CSV for the answer (no subject/discipline columns); optionally use it only to confirm project naming.
assumptions: 'Domain' is operationalized as the 'discipline' column (Social, Cognitive, Economics); it is the only domain-like variable with subjects information and is constant within each pair id.

'Predominantly students' is measured as the share of studies/pairs with subjects=="students"; categories 'anyone', 'community', 'online' and NaN are counted as non-students in the numerator (but included in the denominator).

The quoted 82.4%/80.9% are treated as approximate reference values from the study's source publication, not as values we must reproduce exactly from the CSV; the answer is chosen by which discipline's observed shares align with them.
One row per pair id is the unit of analysis for the main result; subjects.o is constant within every id, so deduplication does not lose original-study information.
uncertainties: The exact 82.4%/80.9% figures could not be reproduced exactly from the CSV under any simple subset/weighting tried (closest: Social pair-level r = 81.1%; overall pair-level o = 82.3%); they most likely come from the source publication's own sample definition, so the domain selection rests on approximate alignment rather than an exact match.
subjects.r varies across labs within 16 ml1/ml3 pair ids, so the replication-study student share depends slightly on the choice of aggregation level (row-level vs pair-level).
The 'drop' flag semantics are not fully documented; 10 pair ids are entirely drop==True and it is uncertain whether the paper's analysis excluded them.

The second CSV contains no subjects/discipline columns, so it cannot corroborate the subject-type figures; if the researcher has study context on how the quoted percentages were computed, it would resolve the residual discrepancy.

payload.answer:
**Hypothesis (final answer):** The domain in which both original and replication studies predominantly used student subjects is **Social** (social psychology, i.e., the "Social" discipline of the original papers). Within the Social discipline, roughly 82–85% of original studies and 78–82% of replication studies used student samples — the closest alignment with the quoted figures (original 82.4%, replication 80.9%). By contrast, Cognitive studies used students less often in the originals (~71–76%), and Economics — although almost entirely student-based (~94–100%) — comprises only 18 small pairs and is far from the quoted percentages. Hence the domain matching the question is Social.

**Explicit caveat (as requested by the researcher):** The exact quoted figures (82.4% / 80.9%) could not be reproduced exactly from the supplied CSV under any simple subset, filter, or weighting we tried; they are treated as approximate values from the source publication. The domain selection rests on the closest alignment between the observed shares and those quoted values, which is unambiguous: Social has the smallest combined distance to (82.4%, 80.9%) at both the pair level (3.8 pp) and the row level (2.6 pp), versus Cognitive (7.6 / 13.9 pp) and Economics (31.1 / 31.1 pp).

RESULT — Average length of original papers: Experimental Economics vs Psychology

FINAL ANSWER (natural-language, grounded in the data):
Original papers in Experimental Economics are substantially longer than those in Psychology. In the dataset, the 18 Experimental Economics originals (project 'ee') average 28.0 pages (median 27.5, SD 7.4, range 16–45), whereas the 97 Psychology originals (project 'rpp') average only 11.2 pages (median 9, SD 6.3, range 1–31) — a gap of roughly 16.8 pages, i.e., economics originals are about 2.5× longer on average. The rpp mean is inflated relative to its median because of short-format articles: 42.3% of rpp papers are ≤7 pages and 55.7% are ≤10 pages (several are just 1–3 pages, reflecting short-report journal formats), which drags the mean down toward the short end while the median (9 pages) better represents the typical paper. Even so, the contrast is robust: by any measure (mean or median), Experimental Economics originals are far longer than Psychology originals in these replication projects.

| Project                        | n (unique originals) | mean  | median | sd   | min | max |
|--------------------------------|----------------------|-------|--------|------|-----|-----|
| Experimental Economics (ee)    | 18                   | 28.00 | 27.5   | 7.37 | 16  | 45  |
| Psychology (rpp)               | 97                   | 11.22 | 9.0    | 6.30 | 1   | 31  |

payload.answer:
Inspection + proposed approach for: "In which domain do the majority of authors tend to be male for both original and replication studies?"

## 1) File inspection (facts)

**File 1 — meta-regression_study_data_heterogeneity_in_replication_projects.csv**
- Shape: **927 rows × 57 columns**.
- Relevant columns present exactly as expected: `id`, `title`, `authors.o`, `discipline`, `project`, `n_authors.o`, `n_authors.r`, `authors_male.o`, `authors_male.r`, `lab_id`.
- `discipline` (no missing): Social = 668 rows, Cognitive = 241, Economics = 18. `project`: ml1 = 592, ml3 = 220, rpp = 97, ee = 18.
- **No missing values** in `discipline`, `authors_male.o`, `authors_male.r`, `id`, `n_authors.o`, `n_authors.r`. `lab_id` missing in 141 rows (all rpp/ee rows presumably — single-lab or non-many-labs projects; harmless for our question).

**File 2 — meta-regression_replication_success_data_heterogeneity_in_replication_projects.csv**
- Shape: **143 rows × 15 columns**. Contains only effect estimates (ro/rr, Fisher-z, SEs, p-values, sample sizes `no`/`nr`) plus `study` and `project` (Psychology 73, Experimental Philosophy 31, Social Sciences 21, Experimental Economics 18).
- **It has NO author-gender or discipline columns at all** — only missingness is `pm_belief` (104 NA).

## 2) authors_male format (facts)
- Both `authors_male.o` and `authors_male.r` are **ratios in [0, 1]** (e.g., 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.667, 1.0), consistent with "Ratio of male authors". No missing values.
- Consistency check vs `n_authors`: for `.o`, ratio × n_authors is integer in **all 927 rows** (ratio is exact male-count/total). For `.r`, 96 rows are non-integer — all in **ml1 with value 0.56** (14/25-style value that doesn't divide the recorded n_authors.r; minor data quirk, doesn't affect a 0.5 threshold). Also 50 ml3 rows have `authors_male.r = 0.515625` (33/64) where n_authors.r = 64 — looks like an aggregated/team-level value. These quirks are worth noting but do not change majority (>0.5) classification materially except being borderline just above 0.5.

## 3) Discipline-level peek (inspection-level, not final analysis)
Using unique O/R pairs (id level, n = 141: Social 74, Cognitive 49, Economics 18) — row level gives same qualitative picture:

| discipline | mean_o | mean_r | frac_o>0.5 | frac_r>0.5 | frac both>0.5 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cognitive | 0.773 | 0.514 | 0.76 | 0.53 | 0.41 |
| Economics | 0.870 | 0.837 | 0.78 | 0.72 | 0.56 |
| Social | 0.734 | 0.506 | 0.57 | 0.53 | 0.30 |

Rough read: **Economics looks like the strongest candidate** (both means well above 0.5; ~56% of pairs majority-male on both sides), Cognitive and Social have replication-side means ≈ 0.51, i.e., near parity. Note Economics has only 18 pairs, so it rests on a small base. All three disciplines have mean_o > 0.5 (male-majority originals everywhere); the differentiator is the replication side.

## 4) Duplicates / join issues (facts)
- 927 rows but only **141 unique `id`** (O/R pairs); 26 ids have multiple rows because many-labs replications have one row per replication lab (`unique (id, lab_id) pairs = 927`). `authors_male.o` and `discipline` never vary within an id (good — O-side and discipline are id-level constants), but `authors_male.r` varies within those 26 multi-lab ids (each lab team differs).
- **Implication:** for "both original and replication" analysis we should either (a) collapse to id level (e.g., take mean replication ratio across labs per id), or (b) analyze at row level treating each lab replication as a unit. The lab-level rows are duplicated for the original side, so id-level collapse is cleaner; row-level gives Many Labs projects heavy weight. This is a real methodological choice — flagged as an uncertainty.
- File 2 joins to File 1 only loosely via project/study name (no common id column, different project labels) — and since it lacks gender/discipline data, **no join is needed**.

## 5) Proposed approach (pending approval)
- **Data:** File 1 only. File 2 plays **no role** for this question (no author-gender, no discipline columns); I'll state this explicitly in the workflow rather than force a join.
- **Operationalization of "majority of authors tend to be male":** a study is male-majority if its male-author ratio > 0.5. "For both original and replication" = both `authors_male.o > 0.5` AND `authors_male.r > 0.5` for the same O/R pair. "Domain/discipline" = `discipline` (Social/Cognitive/Economics).
- **Primary metric:** collapse multi-lab rows to the **id level** (mean `authors_male.r` across labs per id; `authors_male.o` is constant per id), then per discipline compute: mean ratio for o and r, % of pairs where o > 0.5, % where r > 0.5, and **% where both > 0.5**. Answer = discipline with the highest "both > 0.5" share, cross-checked with means (a discipline where both means > 0.5 is the natural-language answer).
- **Sensitivity checks:** (i) row-level (lab-weighted) instead of id-level; (ii) median instead of mean; (iii) strict `> 0.5` vs `>= 0.5` for ties (exactly 0.5 = evenly mixed, treated as NOT male-majority by default). Robustness across these determines how confident the hypothesis is.
- Deliverable: short Python analysis script (pandas), a small summary table, and a natural-language data-grounded hypothesis as the final answer.

## 6) Assumptions & uncertainties
- **Assumption:** `authors_male.*` ratios are (male authors)/(total authors); 0.5 threshold = majority. Exactly 0.5 treated as non-majority (sensitivity-tested). Values like 0.56 and 0.515625 are taken at face value as data quirks.
- **Assumption:** "domain" = `discipline` column (Social/Cognitive/Economics), the only domain-like variable in File 1. File 2's `project` labels are a different taxonomy and lack gender data.
- **Uncertainty:** id-level (one vote per O/R pair) vs row-level (one vote per lab replication) can shift percentages, especially since 26 multi-lab ids are all in ml1/ml3 (mostly Social/Cognitive). I'll report both; primary = id-level.
- **Uncertainty:** Economics n = 18 pairs — small base, so the conclusion for Economics is weaker statistically; I'll note it but the descriptive answer stands.
- **Uncertainty:** `authors_male.r` for multi-lab ids is collapsed by mean; a strict "every lab majority-male" rule would be harsher — noted as sensitivity only if needed.
- **Fact-based caveat:** File 2 is not used; if the researcher intended a different question mapping for File 2, please say so — but inspection shows it cannot answer an author-gender question.

Approval requested for this approach; after approval I'll run the full analysis and deliver the final hypothesis.

HYPOTHESIS (natural language, data-grounded): Among NLSY79 respondents who were ever incarcerated (ever_jailed == 1, n = 289), 1985 wealth — measured at or before incarceration onset, since ever_jailed covers jailings in 1985–1994 — shows stark demographic disparities. The overall median wealth of the ever-incarcerated is only $720 versus $3,600 for never-incarcerated peers (a $2,880, ~80% lower median). Within the ever-incarcerated group, race and sex disparities are large: among jailed men, White men's median wealth ($2,000) is 2.5× that of Black men ($800) and roughly 2.9× that of Hispanic men ($700). By sex, jailed women are nearly uniformly asset-poor — their median wealth is $0 versus $1,000 for jailed men, with ~65% of jailed women (vs ~36% of jailed men) holding zero or negative wealth. Contrasting each jailed group against its never-jailed demographic peers shows the incarceration group is worse off in every cell, but the penalty is not uniform: jailed Hispanic men (median $700 vs $5,000 for never-jailed Hispanic men) and jailed White men ($2,000 vs $5,500) are far below their peers, while jailed Black men's gap ($800 vs $1,500) is smaller in dollars because never-jailed Black men already have low median wealth — indicating that racial wealth disparities precede and compound with incarceration. The data further suggest that among the ever-incarcerated, the usual female wealth advantage seen among White never-jailed peers does not persist in the same form (White jailed women's median $4,100 exceeds jailed White men's $2,000, but this rests on only 12 observations). In short: the ever-incarcerated enter the 1985–1994 jailing window with markedly lower wealth, and within that group Black and Hispanic men and women of all races are at the bottom of the wealth distribution, with women and minority men concentrated at or near zero net worth.

KEY EVIDENCE (executed analysis, analysis_nls_incarceration.py; outputs in outputs/):
- Sample: 12,013 rows × 6 columns, no missing values. race: white 7,099 / black 3,013 / hipanic 1,901 (reported as "Hispanic" in narrative; spelling is a data artifact); sex: 6,164 F / 5,849 M; ever_jailed = 1 for 289 (2.4%).
- composite_wealth_1985: min −$57,587 (negative = net debt, retained as meaningful), max $2,574,706, median $3,400; 3,209 zeros (26.7%) treated as true zero net worth; 649 negatives (5.4%). Among the ever-incarcerated: 114/289 (39.4%) zero and 16/289 (5.5%) negative; per-cell zero-or-negative shares reported as the zero-coding-robust metric (jailed: Black women 81.2%, Hispanic women 88.9%, Black men 44.1%, Hispanic men 46.2%, White men 29.8%, White women 41.7%).
- Ever-jailed race×sex medians: Black men $800 (n=143), Hispanic men $700 (n=52), White men $2,000 (n=57) — stable male cells; Black women $0 (n=16), Hispanic women $0 (n=9), White women $4,100 (n=12) — reported but flagged as UNSTABLE given n=9–16.
- Marginals among ever-jailed: race — White $2,200, Black $320, Hispanic $0; sex — men $1,000, women $0.
- Jailed-vs-never median gaps per cell (jailed − never): Black M −$700, Hispanic M −$4,300, White M −$3,500, Black F −$200, Hispanic F −$2,300, White F −$1,779.

WORKFLOW: (1) load CSV and verify structure/types/missingness; (2) tabulate race, sex, ever_jailed distributions; (3) diagnostics on composite_wealth_1985 (zeros, negatives, range) to justify treating 0 as true zero and negatives as debts; (4) median/mean/zero-share statistics for ever_jailed==1, ever_jailed==0, and full sample by race×sex and marginals; (5) per-cell jailed-vs-never median differences/ratios; (6) synthesis with timing caveat (1985–1994 jailing window vs 1985 wealth), small-cell caveats, and background note that incarceration status in this lineage derives from residence ("Jail"), consistent with ever_jailed.

LIMITATIONS: (a) timing — wealth is measured in 1985, at or before the jailing window, so these are pre-/at-onset disparities, not consequences of completed incarceration; (b) female race×sex cells (n=9–16) are unstable; substantive claims rest on male cells and marginals; (c) zero-coding of wealth=0 cannot be fully distinguished from missingness (26.7% zeros), though the zero-or-negative share metric is robust to this; (d) observational data — disparities are descriptive, not causal.

=== 1. Сводка по данным ===
- 12 013 строк × 6 колонок (race, sex, ever_jailed, composite_wealth_1985/1990/1996). Пропусков нет ни в одной колонке; wealth-переменные — целые, ever_jailed — только {0, 1}.

- sex: female 6164, male 5849.
- ever_jailed=1: 289 человек (2.4%).

- В CSV нет таймингов, годов арестов или полей места жительства (residence) — только бинарный флаг. Резиденс-прокси из твоего контекста («Jail» / место содержания под стражей) к ЭТИМ колонкам неприменимо — подтверждаю как ограничение: проверить кодировку через residence невозможно.
- Косвенный (не диагностический) признак тайминга: у ever_jailed=1 медианное богатство уже в 1985 ниже ($720 vs $3600), и ещё ниже в 1990 ($0) и 1996 ($0). Совместимо и с инкарцерацией до/около 1985, и с изначальным отбором — данные не позволяют разделить.
- Описание переменной («jailed between 1985 to 1994») прямо конфликтует с вопросом «ever incarcerated + wealth in 1985»: часть группы могла быть заключена ПОСЛЕ 1985 → мы описываем disparities в 1985 среди ретроспективно определённых «когда-либо сидевших» (в окне 1985–1994). Ассоциация, не причинность. В данных неразрешимо — фиксирую как главное допущение.

=== 3. composite_wealth_1985: распределение ===
- min −57 587; 649 отрицательных (5.4%); 3 209 нулей (26.7%); медиана 3 400; p75 16 000; p95 116 138; max 2 574 706. Отрицательные (долги) реально есть — composite ведёт себя как нетто-богатство; оставляю без обрезки/винзоризации, иначе при массе нулей медианы исказятся.
- Распределение крайне скошено вправо; медианы в ячейках ever-группы лежат около нуля ($0–$4100) → разрывы будут частично определяться массой нулей.
- Аномалия: 2 056 строк участвуют в полном дублировании (157 групп; есть гигантские группы по 617, 475, 225, 196, 86, 68 строк; 61 дубль-строка с ever_jailed=1). Природа неясна (ID респондента в данных нет). Для медиан дубликаты малоопасны, но сделаю sensitivity-проверку с dedup.

=== 4. Структура групп (ever_jailed=1, медианы 1985; только структура, не выводы) ===
race/sex         n     median 1985   (фон: median у ever_jailed=0)
black female     16      $0              $200
black male       143     $800            $1 500
hipanic female   9       $0              $2 300
hipanic male     52      $700            $5 000
white female     12      $4 100          $5 878.5
white male       57      $2 000          $5 500
(Все ever_jailed=1: n=289, медиана $720.)

=== 5. Предлагаемый план ===
1. Подгруппы: race × sex (6 ячеек) внутри ever_jailed=1 + сводная строка по всей ever-группе; те же ячейки среди ever_jailed=0 — только как фон.
2. Медианы: обычная медиана по подгруппе, wealth без обрезки (отрицательные = долг, нули = отсутствие активов).
3. «Разрывы»: (а) долларовые разницы к референс-группе; (б) относительные (ratio / % разницы) с оговоркой о неустойчивости при медианах ~0; (в) дополнительно доля с нулевым/отрицательным богатством в ячейке — при медианах около нуля это информативнее.
4. Robustness: пересчёт после удаления полных дубликатов; n каждой ячейки в таблице; предупреждение по ячейкам с n<15.
5. Оформление: исполняемый скрипт (артефакт), таблица + natural-language hypothesis по контракту DiscoveryBench; в payload — hypothesis и workflow.

=== Допущения ===
1. ever_jailed = «сидел в окне 1985–1994» по метаданным; тайминг относительно 1985 не наблюдаем → 1985-богатство может относиться и к до-, и к после-инкарцерационному периоду; выводы описательные.

4. Состав пяти wealth-компонент неизвестен — трактую composite как нетто-богатство (подтверждается отрицательными значениями).
5. "hipanic" — репортую как есть, в тексте Hispanic.

## 2. 拟定分析方案

回答"在曾被监禁人群中，1985 年中位财富存在哪些人口统计差异"，步骤如下：

1. **样本口径**：仅取 ever_jailed=1 的 289 人；不剔除缺失值（本数据无缺失）。负值（净财富为负属合法观测，如负债）予以保留，但会报告"剔除负值后的中位数"作为敏感性检验。

INSPECTION REPORT (no modeling run yet) + PROPOSED APPROACH

(1) BASIC STRUCTURE — data/nls_incarceration_processed.csv
- 12,013 rows × 6 columns; zero missing values in every column.
- Columns/dtypes: race (str), sex (str), ever_jailed (int64 0/1), composite_wealth_1985/1990/1996 (int64 dollars).
- Encodings: race ∈ {white 7,099, black 3,013, "hipanic" 1,901 (note the misspelled label, likely 'hispanic')}; sex ∈ {female 6,164, male 5,849}; ever_jailed ∈ {0: 11,724, 1: 289} (2.4% ever jailed). ever_jailed = 1 means jailed sometime in 1985–1994 per the dataset description.
- There is NO separate income column — the only economic variables are the three composite wealth measures. Any "income level" grouping must be constructed from wealth (or is unanswerable as literally stated).

(2) WEALTH DISTRIBUTIONS — heavy-tailed and zero/negative-laden, as suspected
- Overall: 1985 mean 24,673 / median 3,400; 1990 mean 72,563 / median 10,000; 1996 mean 103,400 / median 7,700. Maxima ~$2.5M–$4M; minima as low as −$866,400 (1990). Heavy right tails dominate the means.
- Negatives exist in all three waves (1985: 649 rows; 1990: 614; 1996: 358) and zeros are very common (up to 4,561 rows at zero in 1996). 1990 has a suspicious extreme (−$866,400) consistent with summing raw NLS components where a negative asset (e.g., business/farm debt) dominates. Medians are far more informative than means here; a log(x−min) or rank/winsorized treatment is advisable.
- By race (medians 1985/1990/1996): black $700/$1,000(?) /$4,000; "hipanic" $3,300/…/$16,000; white $5,600/…/$8,850. Means show the same ordering (white ≫ hispanic > black).
- By ever_jailed: jailed respondents are much poorer at every wave (medians 1985: $720 vs $3,600; 1996: $0 vs $8,500), but this is a raw, unadjusted gap.

(3) OVERLAP: ever_jailed window (1985–1994) vs wealth windows
- 1985 wealth is PRE-event for everyone: it precedes the entire jailing window, so it is a valid baseline.
- 1990 wealth is AMBIGUOUS: a respondent jailed in, say, 1986–1989 is already post-event in 1990, while one jailed in 1991–1994 is not. The dataset does not record jailing year, so 1990 cannot be cleanly labeled baseline or post-event — I will treat it as a mid-window "during/ambiguous" checkpoint, not a clean pre/post contrast.
- 1996 wealth is POST-event for all ever_jailed=1 respondents (window ends 1994), but there is 2–11 years of heterogeneity in time since jailing.
- So the cleanest comparison is 1985 (baseline) → 1996 (post), with 1990 reported descriptively only.

(4) FEASIBILITY OF THE black × income-level BREAKDOWN
- Black respondents: 3,013 total; 159 ever jailed, 2,854 not.
- Stratifying black respondents into quartiles of baseline (1985) wealth: jailed group sizes per tier are 45 / 38 / 42 / 34 (non-jailed ~709–719 per tier). This is feasible for quartile-level comparisons (n≈34–45 per jailed cell), though underpowered for fine splits or covariate-adjusted models with many parameters. Tertiles would give ~50+ per jailed cell if more power is needed.

PROPOSED APPROACH (for approval)
1. Restrict to black respondents (n=3,013). Define baseline socioeconomic tier from composite_wealth_1985 — report results for both quartiles and tertiles of the 1985 composite (median-based tiers are distorted by the zero mass: black 1985 quantiles are Q1=$0, median=$700, Q3=$6,300, so I will rank-based-cut the distribution).
2. Within each tier, compare 1985→1996 wealth trajectories for ever_jailed=1 vs 0: (a) medians (primary, robust to tails), (b) means (secondary), (c) the change Δ = wealth_1996 − wealth_1985, and (d) optionally a within-tier difference-in-differences (jailed vs non-jailed change gap), which is the simplest identification we can defend.
3. Descriptive 1990 checkpoint by tier, flagged as ambiguous timing.
4. Robustness: winsorize at the 1st/99th percentile or use log(x − min + 1); exclude/flag the extreme negative outliers (e.g., 1990 min −$866,400); check results using tertiles instead of quartiles; report exact cell sizes everywhere.
5. Output a natural-language hypothesis grounded in the observed tier-specific jailed-vs-non-jailed wealth gaps (e.g., whether the incarceration-associated wealth penalty is larger in magnitude among the higher baseline-wealth tiers and larger in relative terms among lower tiers — to be determined by the actual numbers).

- A1: "Income level" is operationalized as baseline (1985) composite wealth tier, since the dataset has no income variable. (Needs researcher confirmation — see questions.)
- A2: ever_jailed=1 captures any jailing 1985–1994; 1985 wealth is strictly pre-event for all respondents.
- A3: The composite wealth variables are comparable across waves (same five components each year); negative values are legitimate net-worth negatives, except possible data-entry outliers which I will flag rather than silently drop.
- A4: NLSY79 cohort — respondents are young adults in 1985 (cohort aged ~18–27 in 1979, so ~24–33 in 1985), meaning baseline wealth is early-career and trajectories are still steep for everyone.

KEY UNCERTAINTIES / LIMITATIONS (to state in any final answer)
- Selection bias: jailing is not random; jailed respondents already had far lower baseline wealth (mean $7,929 vs $25,086). Stratifying on baseline tier mitigates this but does not eliminate within-tier selection (e.g., unobserved earnings, family background).
- The 1985→1996 change conflates incarceration with aging, macro conditions (early-1990s recession), and the fact that jailed respondents may miss surveys or have different wealth-measurement quality.

- Cell sizes of ~34–45 jailed black respondents per quartile mean tier-specific estimates are noisy; I will emphasize direction and rough magnitude, not precise effects.
- No causal claim is defensible from these data alone; the deliverable is a data-grounded associative hypothesis.

HYPOTHESIS (data-grounded answer to "How does incarceration affect the wealth of black individuals based on their income levels?")

Operationalization (stated explicitly): the dataset contains no income variable, so "income levels" are operationalized as baseline (1985) composite-wealth tiers (quartiles primary, tertiles robustness) among black respondents (n=3,013; 159 ever jailed 1985–1994, 2,854 not).

Hypothesis: Incarceration between 1985 and 1994 is associated with a severe, tier-dependent wealth penalty for black individuals that grows in absolute dollars with baseline wealth but is most complete — near-total wealth non-accumulation — among lower-baseline-wealth respondents. (a) In the lowest baseline tiers, jailed respondents fail to accumulate any wealth at all: median 1985→1996 wealth change is $0 for the jailed vs +$2,000 for non-jailed in the lowest quartile (Q1) and $0 vs $0 in Q2, with 71–79% of jailed respondents still at or below zero wealth in 1996 (vs 46–57% of non-jailed); by 1996 the jailed median is $0 in every tier below the top, versus $1,000–$12,000 for non-jailed peers who started in the same tier. (b) In the upper tiers, incarceration is associated with outright wealth loss: in Q3 the jailed median wealth change is −$1,400 vs +$9,400 for non-jailed (median 1996 wealth $0 vs $12,000), and in the top quartile (Q4) jailed respondents' median wealth falls from ~$15,185 to ~$9,800 (change −$8,000) while matched non-jailed peers gain (+$6,000 change; 1996 median $28,600 vs $9,800). The within-tier difference-in-differences on mean wealth change are approximately −$19K (Q1), −$16K (Q2), −$42K (Q3), and −$58K (Q4), i.e., the absolute incarceration-associated wealth gap roughly triples from the lowest to the highest baseline tier. In relative terms, jailed respondents' 1996 median wealth is essentially zero (ratio ≈ 0) in the low/middle tiers and only 0.34× their non-jailed peers even in the top quartile — so incarceration appears to prevent wealth-building entirely at low income levels and to actively erode existing wealth at higher income levels. Direction is consistent across median and mean, quartile and tertile stratification, and 1%/99% winsorization (winsorized median-change DiD: −$2,000 / $0 / −$10,800 / −$14,900 by quartile).

This is an associative hypothesis, not a causal estimate: jailed respondents were already poorer at baseline within the full sample, jailing is an inferred proxy (residence such as 'Jail'), and no causal identification is possible from these data.
