Inspección completada y propuesta analítica lista para su revisión. No se ha ejecutado el análisis completo.

(1) INSPECCIÓN DEL REPOSITORIO Y DEL DATASET
- Repositorio: solo `data/nls_incarceration_processed.csv` (12.013 filas + cabecera = 12.014 líneas) y `task.json`. No hay scripts previos ni documentación adicional.
- Dimensiones: 12.013 respondientes × 6 columnas, sin valores faltantes en ninguna columna.
- Tipos: race (categórica: white 7.099, black 3.013, "hipanic" [sic, probable typo de "hispanic"] 1.901), sex (female 6.164, male 5.849), ever_jailed (entero 0/1), composite_wealth_1985/1990/1996 (enteros, en dólares).
- ever_jailed por raza/sexo: hombres negros 9,8% (la tasa más alta), hombres hispanos 5,7%, hombres blancos 1,6%; mujeres <1,1% en todos los grupos. Entre los negros hay 159 encarcelados vs 2.854 no encarcelados (grupo tratado pequeño).
- Riqueza: distribuciones muy asimétricas y con atípicos extremos (máx ~2,57M en 1985; ~4,06M en 1990; ~3,84M en 1996). Medianas mucho menores que medias (p. ej. 1996: mediana 7.700 vs media 103.400). Hay valores negativos (patrimonio neto negativo: 649 en 1985, 614 en 1990, 358 en 1996) y muchos ceros exactos (3.209 en 1985, 4.561 en 1996).
- Descriptivos básicos para respondientes negros por ever_jailed:
  - 1985 (pre): media 6.071 (encarcelados) vs 11.054 (no); mediana 320 vs 764.
  - 1990: media 16.967 vs 29.324; mediana 0 vs 3.235.
  - 1996: media 10.393 vs 48.865; mediana 0 vs 5.000.
  - La brecha crece con el tiempo, sobre todo en 1996.
- Tasa de encarcelamiento por cuartil de riqueza 1985 (negros): Q1 5,8%, Q2 3,6%, Q3 5,5%, Q4 4,5% — relativamente pareja, con leve concentración en el cuartil más pobre.

(2) PROPUESTA DE ENFOQUE ANALÍTICO
La pregunta pide el efecto de la encarcelación sobre la riqueza de personas negras según niveles de ingreso. Como no hay columna de ingreso, propongo usar la riqueza de 1985 (pre-tratamiento, dado que ever_jailed cubre 1985–1994) como proxy de posición socioeconómica inicial y estratificar por ella:

1. Muestra: solo respondientes negros (n=3.013).
2. Definir "cambio de riqueza": riqueza en 1990 y 1996 menos riqueza en 1985 (y/o ratios/crecimiento), en niveles y posiblemente en log para atenuar la asimetría.
3. Estratificar por riqueza inicial 1985 en terciles o cuartiles (p. ej., Q1 más pobre … Q4 más rico), y comparar dentro de cada estrato el cambio mediano (y de media con winsorización o recorte de atípicos, p. ej. al percentil 99) entre ever_jailed=1 y ever_jailed=0.
4. Complementar con una regresión (p. ej., OLS sobre cambio de riqueza con interacción ever_jailed × estrato de riqueza inicial, controles por sexo) para cuantificar la heterogeneidad del efecto según nivel socioeconómico inicial, reportando el efecto diferencial por estrato.
5. Salida: tabla de cambios de riqueza (mediana y media) encarcelados vs no encarcelados por estrato para negros, más el contraste de la hipótesis final en lenguaje natural.

Nota: también puedo comparar la magnitud del efecto entre razas como contexto, pero el foco del entregable será el grupo negro.

(3) SUPUESTOS Y DUDAS
- ever_jailed = encarcelado en algún momento entre 1985 y 1994; el cambio 1985→1990 mezcla pre y post-tratamiento (tratamiento parcialmente "en curso"); 1985 es razonablemente pre-tratamiento, 1996 claramente post.
- No hay ingreso directo: uso la riqueza 1985 como proxy del nivel de ingreso/situación socioeconómica; esto es un supuesto clave que puede alterar la interpretación de "según niveles de ingreso".
- La riqueza compuesta es la suma de solo 5 variables de NLS (posiblemente activos sin restar deudas de forma completa, o con componentes codificados 0); los numerosos ceros exactos y negativos sugieren medición gruesa. La calidad de esta variable limita la precisión.
- Selección fuerte: la encarcelación no es aleatoria y los encarcelados parten con ~45% menos riqueza media en 1985; sin covariables adicionales solo puedo hacer comparaciones descriptivas/condicionales al baseline, no causalidad.
- Grupo tratado pequeño (n=159 negros encarcelados): los estratos con pocos casos tendrán estimaciones ruidosas; usaré medianas y reportaré tamaños de celda.
- Atípicos y valores negativos: definiré reglas explícitas (p. ej. winsorizar al 1%/99% y reportar también medianas, robustas a ambos).
- Duda abierta para usted: ¿prefiere el análisis estratificado solo para negros, o también un contraste entre razas como contexto? Y ¿desea usar terciles o cuartiles de riqueza 1985 como "niveles de ingreso"? Por defecto propongo terciles y foco en negros.

HYPOTHESIS (data-grounded, descriptive — answering "How does incarceration affect the wealth of black individuals based on their income levels?"):

Among Black respondents in the NLSY79 data, incarceration is associated with a near-complete stall — and for those who started with some wealth, an outright reversal — of wealth accumulation, and the setback scales with initial socioeconomic position. Stratifying Black respondents (n=3,013; 159 ever jailed) by terciles of 1985 baseline wealth as a proxy for income level: in the lowest tercile (1985 median wealth ≈ $0), jailed respondents remain pinned at $0 median wealth through 1996, capturing only ~30% of the wealth growth their non-jailed peers achieve ($6,077 vs $20,203 mean change, winsorized). In the middle tercile, jailed respondents' median wealth change by 1996 is negative (−$1,000) versus +$6,231 for non-jailed peers; in the highest tercile it is strongly negative (−$5,800) versus +$8,825, meaning jailed respondents in the top tercile end 1996 with less wealth than they had in 1985. The absolute wealth gap between ever-jailed and never-jailed Black respondents widens monotonically with initial wealth: ≈$14K (low), ≈$28K (mid), ≈$52K (high) in winsorized mean 1985→1996 change, and an OLS on winsorized 1996 change with a jailed×tercile interaction (controlling sex) confirms the penalty is significantly more negative in the top tercile (interaction −$35.2K, p=0.017). Thus, contrary to the intuition that the poor are hit hardest, the dollar and proportional wealth setback from incarceration is largest for Black individuals who started with mid-to-high wealth, while for the poorest third incarceration is associated with being locked out of wealth accumulation entirely (median wealth stuck at $0). All comparisons are descriptive associations, not causal effects: the jailed group already had less wealth in 1985, the treatment window (1985–1994) overlaps the 1985→1990 change, and the composite wealth measure is coarse (many exact zeros/negatives).

Brief race context (optional, as agreed): the pattern of jailed respondents' median 1996 wealth collapsing to $0 holds for all races (white: $9,000 vs $0; hispanic: $17,075 vs $0), but incarceration rates are far higher among Black men (9.8%) than white (1.6%) or hispanic (5.7%) men, so the racial incidence of the exposure differs even if the within-group wealth pattern is similar.

PLAN — NLS incarceration × wealth analysis (inspection complete; no full analysis run yet)

== 1. DATA INSPECTION (data/nls_incarceration_processed.csv) ==

Structure: 12,013 data rows × 6 columns; header matches the documented schema exactly: race, sex, ever_jailed, composite_wealth_1985, composite_wealth_1990, composite_wealth_1996. All numeric columns parse cleanly as integers; no NaNs anywhere (0 missing in every column).

race (3 levels): white 7,099 | black 3,013 | "hipanic" 1,901 (note: misspelled label for hispanic — kept as-is, no recode needed for our purposes).
sex: female 6,164 | male 5,849.
ever_jailed: 0 = 11,724 (97.6%) | 1 = 289 (2.4%). By race×sex among black respondents: 159/3,013 (5.3%) ever jailed — 143 black males (9.8% of black males) vs only 16 black females (1.0%).

Wealth variables (all rows):
- composite_wealth_1985: mean 24,673; median 3,400; IQR [0, 16,000]; min −57,587; max 2,574,706; 649 negative values; 3,209 zeros.
- composite_wealth_1990: mean 72,563; median 10,000; IQR [0, 70,600]; min −866,400; max 4,060,077; 614 negative; 2,975 zeros.
- composite_wealth_1996: mean 103,400; median 7,700; IQR [0, 115,000]; min −403,001; max 3,836,910; 358 negative; 4,561 zeros.
Zero/negative handling decision: negatives are retained (composite net worth can legitimately be negative — debts exceed assets; they are not missing-value codes) and zeros are retained (the 25th percentile is 0, so zero wealth is a mass point, not an error). I will not drop or floor them; for skewed-scale summaries I will report medians/IQR and, where a log scale helps, use signed transforms (sign(w)·log1p(|w|)) or quantile ranks rather than deleting nonpositive values.

Duplicates: 1,899 rows are exact duplicates of another row (12,013 → 10,114 unique). This is consequential and needs a decision (see assumptions) — NLSY extracts should have one row per respondent, so duplicates may be a processing artifact. I propose deduplicating for the primary analysis and reporting sensitivity with duplicates retained.

Black subgroup (n=3,013; 2,854 never-jailed vs 159 jailed):
- 1985 wealth: jailed mean 6,071 / median 320 vs never-jailed mean 11,054 / median 764 → jailed start poorer.
- 1990: jailed mean 16,967 / median 0 vs 29,324 / 3,235.
- 1996: jailed mean 10,393 / median 0 vs 48,865 / 5,000 → the gap widens sharply by 1996 (jailed median wealth stays at 0; never-jailed grows ~6.5×).
This raw pattern (already visible from inspection alone, not yet formally analyzed) motivates the hypothesis.

== 2. OTHER STAGED ASSETS ==

The environment contains only two items besides the dataset:
- task.json — the benchmark episode definition (same content as the public task: question, datasets.json schema document, submission contract). No additional code, notebooks, documentation, or data dictionaries are staged.
- data/nls_incarceration_processed.csv — the sole data asset (343 KB).
So there is no hidden income variable or codebook beyond the schema in datasets.json; the five constituent wealth variables are not provided, only their composite sums.

== 3. PROPOSED ANALYTICAL APPROACH ==

Question: "How does incarceration affect the wealth of black individuals based on their income levels?"

(a) Race/sex restriction and stratification
- Primary sample: race == 'black' (n=3,013; n=1,011 unique after dedup estimate — I'll verify exact unique counts within black).
- Sex stratification: primary analysis on black MALES (the jailed group is 143 of 159; black females have only 16 jailed cases — underpowered). Secondary/secondary-stratum analysis on all black respondents and on black females, reported with explicit small-n caveats.
- Optionally use white respondents as a descriptive comparison group for context, but the hypothesis itself concerns black individuals.

(b) Wealth change relative to the 1985–1994 jailing window
Define, per respondent:
- Δ_early = composite_wealth_1990 − composite_wealth_1985 (1985→1990; note 1990 falls MID-window, since jailing spans 1985–1994 — see assumptions);
- Δ_late = composite_wealth_1996 − composite_wealth_1990 (1990→1996; mostly post-window);
- Δ_total = composite_wealth_1996 − composite_wealth_1985 (whole arc).
Compare jailed vs never-jailed black respondents on these changes, controlling for baseline: the cleanest estimand is the 1985→1996 change conditional on 1985 wealth (and sex), i.e., a simple difference-in-differences style comparison / OLS of Δ_total ~ ever_jailed × baseline-tier + sex, plus median (quantile) comparisons because the wealth distribution is extremely right-skewed. Also report the trajectory of median wealth by year (1985/1990/1996) for jailed vs non-jailed within each stratum.

(c) Wealth levels vs "income" stratification — handling the absence of an income variable
The files contain wealth but no income variable. I will not fabricate an income measure. Instead I will use BASELINE (1985) composite wealth as the socioeconomic-status proxy and stratify black respondents into baseline wealth tiers, e.g.:
- Tier 0: zero/negative wealth in 1985 (no assets);
- Tier 1: low positive (0 < w ≤ median of positives);
- Tier 2: middle (median–75th pct);
- Tier 3: high (>75th pct / top decile).
Within each tier, compare 1985→1990→1996 wealth trajectories and changes for ever_jailed=1 vs 0. This directly answers "based on their income levels" in the only data-grounded way available: does incarceration hurt wealth more for those who started with little (expected: trapped at/near zero wealth, e.g., jailed median stays 0 through 1996) than for those who started with more (expected: smaller relative but larger absolute losses)? Wealth remains a LEVEL outcome in dollars (with signed-log/quantile transforms for modeling); baseline wealth serves only as the stratifier standing in for income.

Execution plan: a single Python script (pandas; statsmodels if available, else manual OLS/robust comparisons) producing (i) a summary table of wealth levels and deltas by ever_jailed × baseline-tier × sex, (ii) regression/quantile estimates with the jailed×tier interaction, (iii) the natural-language hypothesis grounded in these numbers, saved as the artifact.

== 4. CONSEQUENTIAL ASSUMPTIONS AND UNCERTAINTIES ==

1. ever_jailed construction — FACT vs ASSUMPTION, per your study note: The dataset's own schema (datasets.json, staged in task.json) documents ever_jailed as "equals 1 if the respondent was jailed between 1985 to 1994." I can verify only that it is a 0/1 variable consistent with that description (2.4% incidence, strongly male-skewed, plausible for 1985–1994 NLSY79). The file contains NO residence or facility variable, so I CANNOT verify from this data whether jailing was inferred from residence recorded as 'Jail' — that mechanism remains an upstream assumption about how the processed variable was built; my analysis treats the documented definition ("jailed 1985–1994") as given.
2. No income variable: baseline wealth is a proxy for income tier, not income itself. Wealth and income are correlated but distinct; conclusions are about wealth-tier heterogeneity, not literal income. This is the main limitation for the question's phrasing.
3. Timing mismatch: jailing is dated 1985–1994, but the intermediate wealth measurement is 1990 — mid-window. Δ_early mixes pre- and post-incarceration change for some respondents; only 1996 is unambiguously post-window for all jailed respondents. I will interpret Δ_late/Δ_total as the primary outcomes.
4. Observational design, small treated group: 159 jailed black respondents (143 male). ever_jailed is not random; jailed respondents already had lower baseline wealth (mean 6,071 vs 11,054 in 1985). All effects will be framed as associations/hypotheses, not causal estimates, and I will explicitly condition on baseline wealth to mitigate (not eliminate) baseline selection.
5. Duplicates: 1,899 exact duplicate rows. Assumption: they are a processing artifact and should be deduplicated for the primary analysis; I will run a sensitivity check with duplicates retained and disclose if conclusions change.
6. Composite wealth: it is a sum of five NLSY wealth items I cannot see; component-level missingness handling in the upstream processing is unobservable. Negative and zero values are kept as valid net-worth states (assumption: no negative value is an error code; the minima, e.g., −866,400 in 1990, are plausible debt levels).
7. Outliers: extreme right tail (max $3.8M among black respondents) will dominate means; hence medians/quantiles and signed-log transforms are primary, means secondary.
8. The 'hipanic' label is a typo in the source data; it does not affect the black-only primary analysis.

One executed Python script + outputs, and a final natural-language hypothesis, e.g., of the form "Among black NLSY79 respondents, incarceration (jailing 1985–1994) is associated with near-zero wealth traps for those starting with little/zero wealth, and [quantified] losses for those starting with more — with the effect concentrated in X tier," with all numbers filled from the executed analysis.

payload.answer:
HYPOTHESIS (natural language, data-grounded)

"Among black NLSY79 respondents, being jailed between 1985 and 1994 is associated with a substantial and persistent loss of wealth, and the form of that loss depends on the respondent's economic starting point — operationalized here as baseline 1985 composite wealth tier, which stands in for income level because the dataset contains no income variable. Black individuals who started with little or no wealth (1985 wealth below the 75th percentile, ≈$9,200) were driven to and trapped at zero net worth: median 1996 wealth among the jailed was $0 in every tier below the top, versus $5,000–$16,850 among otherwise comparable never-jailed peers, and 55–67% of jailed respondents in those tiers remained at ≤$0 wealth in 1996 versus only 18–31% of never-jailed peers. Black individuals who started in the top wealth tier (>≈$24,900 in 1985) largely avoided the zero-wealth trap but suffered the largest absolute losses: median 1985→1996 wealth change of −$9,500 versus +$6,900 for never-jailed peers, with the divergence concentrated in the post-window period (1990→1996 median change of +$300 vs +$10,800 among black men). Regression estimates conditioning on baseline wealth tier and sex put the jailed-vs-never-jailed penalty in 1985→1996 wealth change at ≈−$34,000 in the lowest tier, growing to ≈−$65,000 in the highest tier (all p<0.001; signed-log outcomes −3.7 to −7.4 log-points, all p<0.05) — i.e., the absolute dollar penalty rises with starting wealth, while the relative devastation (collapse to zero) hits those who started with the least. The association is concentrated among black men (113 of 124 jailed cases) and is robust to retaining duplicate records; because jailed respondents were already poorer at baseline and incarceration is not randomly assigned, this is an association, not a causal effect."

WORKFLOW (executed, analysis.py)
1. Loaded data/nls_incarceration_processed.csv (12,013 rows × 6 cols; 0 missing; schema matches datasets.json). Deduplicated exact rows: 1,899 dropped → 10,114 unique overall; black subgroup = 2,465 unique rows (correction to my provisional n=1,011 estimate), jailed black = 124 after dedup (35 of the 159 raw jailed black rows were duplicates). Sensitivity analysis with duplicates retained (n=3,013, jailed=159) run in parallel.
2. Defined outcomes: d_early = w1990−w1985 (mid-window, ambiguous), d_late = w1996−w1990 (primary), d_total = w1996−w1985 (primary); signed-log transform sign(x)·log1p(|x|) for scale robustness. Negatives and zeros retained as valid net-worth states.
3. Stratifier ("income levels" proxy): baseline 1985 composite wealth tiers computed on the primary black dedup sample — Tier 0: ≤$0; Tier 1: $0–$5,400 (median of positives); Tier 2: $5,400–$9,200 (p75); Tier 3: >$24,899 (above p90 gap).
4. Strata: primary = all black dedup (n=2,465) and black males dedup (n=1,206, jailed=113); context = black females (n=1,259, jailed=11 — small-n caveat); sensitivity = all black rows with duplicates; comparison = white males (context only).
5. Estimation: tier×jailed median-trajectory tables (medians, % ending ≤$0, % ending below baseline) plus OLS with HC3 robust SEs for d_total and sl_total ~ C(tier)·ever_jailed (+ sex where applicable). Tables exported to 5 CSVs.

KEY EVIDENCE (primary: black, deduplicated)
Tier × jailed medians (w1985→w1990→w1996; Δ_total median; % ≤$0 in 1996):
- Tier 0 (n=756 vs 48): 0→2,400→5,000 vs 0→0→0; Δ +5,732 vs 0; 30% vs 60% at ≤$0.
- Tier 1 (793 vs 38): 1,905→5,500→10,000 vs 1,662→0→0; Δ +8,000 vs 0; 30% vs 60%.
- Tier 2 (205 vs 9): 7,000→11,000→16,000 vs 6,280→3,500→0; Δ +9,050 vs −5,800; 20% vs 70%.
- Tier 3 (587 vs 29): 20,035→24,450→36,000 vs 16,000→4,600→11,000; Δ +6,900 vs −9,500; 20% vs 30%.
Black males (primary stratum) show the same pattern amplified: Tier 3 Δ_total median +12,700 vs −9,650; 1990→1996 median +10,800 vs +300.
OLS Δ_total ~ tier×jailed+sex (black dedup, HC3): jailed×tier = −34,028 (p=0.0005), −39,530 (p<0.0001), −63,462 (p<0.0001), −65,278 (p=0.0001) for tiers 0–3; signed-log coefficients −5.0/−5.1/−7.4/−3.7, all p<0.05.
Sensitivity (duplicates retained, n=3,013): all coefficients and medians directionally identical (e.g., Tier 3 Δ_total median −9,500 vs +6,450; jailed×tier −21,270 to −63,918, all p≤0.001 except tier3 signed-log p=0.056) — conclusions unchanged.
White males (context): jailed penalties also large (−$96k to −$145k in dollars) but the zero-wealth trap is less universal; the black-specific pattern of median $0 outcomes in tiers 0–2 is distinctive.

LIMITATIONS / CARRIED CAVEATS
- ever_jailed is documented as "jailed 1985–1994"; the upstream residence='Jail' inference mechanism cannot be verified from this file (no residence column) and remains an assumption.
- 1990 wealth is measured mid-window; d_early mixes pre/post periods — d_late and d_total are the primary outcomes, as agreed.
- No income variable: baseline wealth tier is the income proxy, stated explicitly in the hypothesis.
- Observational, baseline selection (jailed started poorer: 1985 mean $6,071 vs $11,054 among black); conditioning on baseline tier mitigates but does not eliminate confounding — associations only.
- Small cells: black females jailed n=11 after dedup (tier cells of 1–8); Tier 2 jailed n=9 (males). Direction consistent but imprecise.
- Duplicates: primary dedup per your decision; sensitivity confirms robustness. 'hipanic' typo carries no effect on the black-only analysis.
- Composite wealth is a sum of five unseen component variables; upstream missingness handling unobservable.

Artifacts: analysis.py (executed, nonempty) + 5 exported tables.

HYPOTHESIS (natural-language, data-grounded)

Among black NLSY79 respondents, incarceration (ever_jailed, 1985–1994) is associated with substantially slower wealth accumulation and a higher probability of ending with no positive wealth — and the association is largest for those who were not at the very bottom to begin with. Because the dataset contains no income variable, "income levels" are proxied by baseline (1985) composite wealth, stratified into terciles within the black subsample (T1 ≤ $0; T2 $0–$3,830; T3 > $3,830).

By 1996, within every baseline-wealth stratum, ever-jailed black respondents are worse off than never-jailed peers with the same starting position:
- Lowest tercile (T1, jailed n=76 vs never n=1,240): baseline wealth is effectively zero for both (median $0). By 1996 the jailed group's mean wealth is $6,093 vs $23,274 (gap −$17,181; winsorized −$14,326), and only 22% hold positive wealth vs 45% of the never-jailed. Median differences are masked at $0 by floor effects, so this stratum shows the incarceration association mainly as a halving of the chance of accumulating any wealth.
- Middle tercile (T2, jailed n=39 vs never n=654): starting positions are statistically indistinguishable (medians both $1,400; p=0.85). By 1996 the jailed median falls to $0 while the never-jailed median rises to $7,450 (gap −$7,450); mean gap −$29,393 (winsorized −$28,252). Positive-wealth share: 38% vs 72%. DiD-style mean change 1985→1996: +$10,196 (jailed) vs +$39,587 (never), a gap of −$29,391.
- Highest tercile (T3, jailed n=44 vs never n=960): despite comparable 1985 wealth (medians $11,150 vs $11,900; MWU p=0.99), the jailed group's median wealth drops from $11,150 (1985) to $4,700 (1996) — it does not grow at all — while the never-jailed median rises to $26,750. Median gap −$22,050; DiD mean-change gap −$59,008; positive-wealth share 55% vs 78%. This is the largest relative setback: incarceration is associated with a complete arrest of wealth growth among those who began with meaningful assets.

The gradient is thus U-shaped in relative terms: at the floor (T1) there is little wealth left to lose (a "nothing-to-lose" floor effect compresses level differences but halves the probability of any accumulation), while in the mid and upper terciles the jailed group loses both the level and the growth trajectory — median 1996 wealth is $0 (T2) or $4,700 (T3) versus $7,450 and $26,750 for never-jailed peers, with rank-based tests significant in all strata (MWU p<0.001 for 1990 and 1996 in T2/T3, p<0.001 in T1 for levels despite $0 medians).

Robustness and checks: quartile robustness was run where jailed cell sizes stayed ≥30 (Q1 n=76, Q3 n=42, Q4 n=34); Q2 was skipped (jailed n=7 < 30). Quartiles confirm the pattern (e.g., Q3: 1996 median −$12,000, DiD mean gap −$41,495; Q4: median −$19,075, DiD gap −$58,632). Winsorization at the 99th percentile leaves mean gaps essentially unchanged, and the positive-wealth indicator shows the same ordering. Sex-stratified check: jailing is heavily male-concentrated among black respondents (143/1,465 men vs 16/1,548 women jailed), yet the negative association appears in both sexes (male DiD mean gap 1985→1996 −$39,526; female −$30,529, based on only 16 jailed women), and a sex-demeaned pooled comparison among black respondents yields a 1996 gap of −$42,189 — so the pattern is not a male-only artifact. White reference contrast: the same within-stratum pattern appears among white respondents (e.g., T3 jailed n=13: median falls from $30,000 to $12,200 while never-jailed rises $48,000→$106,000), suggesting incarceration is associated with wealth loss across races; the black–white gap in levels persists at every stratum regardless of jailing.

In short: incarceration is associated with a wealth penalty for black individuals at every baseline wealth/income position, but it is expressed differently across the distribution — near the bottom it manifests as a sharply lower probability of accumulating any positive wealth (22% vs 45% by 1996), while in the middle and especially the top of the baseline distribution it manifests as stagnant or negative wealth growth (medians falling from $1,400→$0 and $11,150→$4,700 respectively), i.e., a complete forfeiture of the wealth accumulation that otherwise-stratified peers achieve.

payload.answer:
HYPOTHESIS (natural-language, data-grounded)

Among black NLSY79 respondents, incarceration (ever_jailed, 1985–1994) is associated with substantially slower wealth accumulation and a higher probability of ending with no positive wealth — and the association is largest for those who were not at the very bottom to begin with. Because the dataset contains no income variable, "income levels" are proxied by baseline (1985) composite wealth, stratified into terciles within the black subsample (T1 ≤ $0; T2 $0–$3,830; T3 > $3,830).

By 1996, within every baseline-wealth stratum, ever-jailed black respondents are worse off than never-jailed peers with the same starting position:
- Lowest tercile (T1, jailed n=76 vs never n=1,240): baseline wealth is effectively zero for both (median $0). By 1996 the jailed group's mean wealth is $6,093 vs $23,274 (gap −$17,181; winsorized −$14,326), and only 22% hold positive wealth vs 45% of the never-jailed. Median differences are masked at $0 by floor effects, so this stratum shows the incarceration association mainly as a halving of the chance of accumulating any wealth.
- Middle tercile (T2, jailed n=39 vs never n=654): starting positions are statistically indistinguishable (medians both $1,400; p=0.85). By 1996 the jailed median falls to $0 while the never-jailed median rises to $7,450 (gap −$7,450); mean gap −$29,393 (winsorized −$28,252). Positive-wealth share: 38% vs 72%. DiD-style mean change 1985→1996: +$10,196 (jailed) vs +$39,587 (never), a gap of −$29,391.
- Highest tercile (T3, jailed n=44 vs never n=960): despite comparable 1985 wealth (medians $11,150 vs $11,900; MWU p=0.99), the jailed group's median wealth drops from $11,150 (1985) to $4,700 (1996) — it does not grow at all — while the never-jailed median rises to $26,750. Median gap −$22,050; DiD mean-change gap −$59,008; positive-wealth share 55% vs 78%. This is the largest relative setback: incarceration is associated with a complete arrest of wealth growth among those who began with meaningful assets.

The gradient is thus U-shaped in relative terms: at the floor (T1) there is little wealth left to lose (a "nothing-to-lose" floor effect compresses level differences but halves the probability of any accumulation), while in the mid and upper terciles the jailed group loses both the level and the growth trajectory — median 1996 wealth is $0 (T2) or $4,700 (T3) versus $7,450 and $26,750 for never-jailed peers, with rank-based tests significant in all strata (MWU p<0.001 for 1990 and 1996 in T2/T3, p<0.001 in T1 for levels despite $0 medians).

Robustness and checks: quartile robustness was run where jailed cell sizes stayed ≥30 (Q1 n=76, Q3 n=42, Q4 n=34); Q2 was skipped (jailed n=7 < 30). Quartiles confirm the pattern (e.g., Q3: 1996 median −$12,000, DiD mean gap −$41,495; Q4: median −$19,075, DiD gap −$58,632). Winsorization at the 99th percentile leaves mean gaps essentially unchanged, and the positive-wealth indicator shows the same ordering. Sex-stratified check: jailing is heavily male-concentrated among black respondents (143/1,465 men vs 16/1,548 women jailed), yet the negative association appears in both sexes (male DiD mean gap 1985→1996 −$39,526; female −$30,529, based on only 16 jailed women), and a sex-demeaned pooled comparison among black respondents yields a 1996 gap of −$42,189 — so the pattern is not a male-only artifact. White reference contrast: the same within-stratum pattern appears among white respondents (e.g., T3 jailed n=13: median falls from $30,000 to $12,200 while never-jailed rises $48,000→$106,000), suggesting incarceration is associated with wealth loss across races; the black–white gap in levels persists at every stratum regardless of jailing.

In short: incarceration is associated with a wealth penalty for black individuals at every baseline wealth/income position, but it is expressed differently across the distribution — near the bottom it manifests as a sharply lower probability of accumulating any positive wealth (22% vs 45% by 1996), while in the middle and especially the top of the baseline distribution it manifests as stagnant or negative wealth growth (medians falling from $1,400→$0 and $11,150→$4,700 respectively), i.e., a complete forfeiture of the wealth accumulation that otherwise-stratified peers achieve.

This is an observational association, not a causal estimate: jailing status covers 1985–1994 (so the 1990 comparison is contemporaneous with the jailing window, not a clean pre/post), the composite's construction and units are undocumented, ~30–41% of wealth values are ≤0 (floor effects), treated cells are small (39–76 per tercile), sex is the only available covariate, and the processed file's zero missingness precludes assessing panel attrition.

Inspection report and proposed analysis plan for "Between which years did the largest increases in median wealth occur among black females?" — NOT yet executing the full solution.

## (1) Data inspection — data/nls_incarceration_processed.csv
- **12,013 rows × 6 columns**; dtypes: race=str, sex=str, ever_jailed=int64, composite_wealth_1985/1990/1996=int64.
- **No missing values in any column** (0 NaNs everywhere). Values are already coded, so no NA handling is needed.
- **race**: white 7,099; black 3,013; "hipanic" 1,901 (note: misspelled "hispanic" in the raw file — only matters if we filter by hispanic; irrelevant to this question but worth documenting).
- **sex**: female 6,164; male 5,849. **ever_jailed**: 0 = 11,724, 1 = 289 (not needed for this question).

Composite wealth summary (all rows):
| column | min | q01 | q05 | q25 | median | q75 | q95 | max | n<0 | n=0 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1985 | −57,587 | −5,063 | −320 | 0 | 3,400 | 16,000 | 116,138 | 2,574,706 | 649 | 3,209 |
| 1990 | −866,400 | −10,000 | −200 | 0 | 10,000 | 70,600 | 293,049 | 4,060,077 | 614 | 2,975 |
| 1996 | −403,001 | −8,576 | 0 | 0 | 7,700 | 115,000 | 428,205 | 3,836,910 | 358 | 4,561 |

**Oddities flagged:** (a) negative composite wealth exists (net worth can be negative because the composite sums assets and debts — this is economically valid, not data corruption); (b) extreme outliers up to ±$0.9–4M, likely real high-wealth respondents but a single −$866k value in 1990 suggests possible extreme debt coding; (c) heavy mass at exactly 0 (27–38% of rows) — wealth is coarsely measured; (d) because the composite is a signed sum, **interval changes and percent changes behave very differently near zero** (e.g., $175 → $2,600 is a +1386% change but only +$2,425 in dollars), which is the key methodological risk here.

## (2) Black female subgroup (race=='black' & sex=='female')
- Full sample: 12,013 → black: 3,013 → black females: **1,548**.
- Medians: **1985 = $175; 1990 = $2,600; 1996 = $4,000**.
- **1985→1990: +$2,425 (+1,385.7% relative to $175).**
- **1990→1996: +$1,400 (+53.8%).**
- So in **both dollar and percent terms, 1985→1990 is the largest increase** for black females — the two definitions agree here, which is convenient. Caveat: the percent figure is inflated by the tiny $175 base (median sits inside a large zero-mass cluster).

## (3) Proposed approach
- **Primary definition: dollar change in median wealth** between consecutive intervals (1985→1990, 1990→1996), computed as difference of medians; report percent change alongside as a secondary metric.
- **Primary comparison: within black females only** (the question is explicitly about black females). **Context (secondary, clearly labeled):** the same median table across all six race×sex subgroups, since it materially strengthens the hypothesis — notably, black females are the only group besides hispanic females whose 1990→1996 median change is still positive; white females/males *decline* in 1990→1996 medians (−$11,275 and −$6,701).
- **Missing/nonpositive wealth:** no missing values exist. For the headline result I will **keep all respondents (negatives and zeros included)** — negative net worth is meaningful and median is robust to outliers, so no trimming is needed. I will report a **sensitivity check restricted to wealth > 0** (black female medians become $4,800 / $11,057 / $25,050, i.e., 1985→1990 +$6,257 (+130%) vs 1990→1996 +$13,993 (+127%) — nearly a tie, and the "largest interval" flips to 1990→1996 in dollars). This shows the headline answer is robust at the full-sample definition but sensitive to exclusion choices; I will state both.

## (4) Consequential assumptions and uncertainties
1. **Assumption (documented):** "largest increase" = largest change in median wealth between consecutive survey waves 1985→1990 and 1990→1996 for black females; dollar change is primary. Under this definition the answer is **1985→1990** (+$2,425, +1,386%), robust to both dollar and percent metrics.
2. **Uncertainty — interval spacing:** 1985→1990 and 1990→1996 are both 5–6 year gaps, roughly comparable, so interval comparison is defensible; but the 1996 wave is ~1 year longer, which slightly favors 1990→1996 and does not change the ranking here.
3. **Uncertainty — cross-year comparability:** each composite is a sum of five NLS wealth variables for that year; the datasets.json does not document which five variables or whether item sets/definitions are identical across 1985/1990/1996. If item sets differ, cross-year changes partly reflect measurement, not economics. Undocumented in metadata.
4. **Uncertainty — base-year sensitivity:** the 1985 median ($175) sits in a large zero-mass cluster; small coding shifts would swing percent change dramatically. The dollar-based conclusion is more stable than the percent-based one.
5. **Uncertainty — sensitivity to nonpositive exclusion:** excluding wealth ≤ 0 makes 1990→1996 the (marginally) larger dollar interval (+$13,993 vs +$6,257). The primary full-sample answer (1985→1990) should be stated together with this caveat.
6. **Fact:** race category "hipanic" is misspelled in the data; no missing data; ever_jailed is available but unused (question does not condition on incarceration status).

**Planned final deliverable (after approval):** an executed script producing the median table, interval changes, subgroup context table, and sensitivity check; final answer = natural-language hypothesis: *"Among black females, median wealth rose most between 1985 and 1990 (from $175 to $2,600, +$2,425, ~+1,386%), versus +$1,400 (+54%) between 1990 and 1996; black females were among the few subgroups whose median wealth kept rising in 1990–1996 while white respondents' medians declined."*

payload.answer:
**Hypothesis (final answer):** Among black females in the NLSY79 cohort, median composite wealth increased the most between **1985 and 1990** — rising from $175 to $2,600, an increase of **+$2,425 (+1,386%)** — whereas the 1990→1996 increase was smaller (+$1,400, +54%, from $2,600 to $4,000). This holds under both dollar and percent definitions of "largest increase" in the full sample (all 1,548 black females retained, negative and zero wealth included). The 1985–1990 boom likely reflects the small 1985 base (median inside a large zero-wealth cluster); and notably, black females were among the only subgroups whose median wealth kept rising during 1990–1996, while white respondents' medians declined. **Caveat:** restricting to respondents with positive wealth flips the ranking — the 1990→1996 increase (+$13,993, +127%) marginally exceeds 1985→1990 (+$6,257, +130% percent-wise larger but smaller in dollars), so the conclusion is sensitive to the treatment of nonpositive wealth.

## (1) Median table and interval changes — black females (n = 1,548 of 3,013 black, 12,013 total)
| Year | Median composite wealth |
|---|---|
| 1985 | $175 |
| 1990 | $2,600 |
| 1996 | $4,000 |
- **1985→1990: +$2,425 (+1,385.7%)** ← largest increase
- **1990→1996: +$1,400 (+53.8%)**

## (2) Context — all six race × sex subgroups (labeled as context, not the primary comparison)
| subgroup | n | med 1985 | med 1990 | med 1996 | Δ85→90 $ | Δ90→96 $ | Δ85→90 % | Δ90→96 % |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| black/female | 1,548 | 175 | 2,600 | 4,000 | +2,425 | +1,400 | +1,385.7 | +53.8 |
| black/male | 1,465 | 1,400 | 3,300 | 4,200 | +1,900 | +900 | +135.7 | +27.3 |
| hipanic/female | 986 | 2,200 | 7,649 | 16,750 | +5,449 | +9,101 | +247.7 | +119.0 |
| hipanic/male | 915 | 4,410 | 8,400 | 14,000 | +3,990 | +5,600 | +90.5 | +66.7 |
| white/female | 3,630 | 5,852.5 | 20,100 | 8,825 | +14,247.5 | −11,275 | +243.4 | −56.1 |
| white/male | 3,469 | 5,400 | 15,601 | 8,900 | +10,201 | −6,701 | +188.9 | −43.0 |

Context reading: black females had the lowest wealth levels throughout but positive median growth in both intervals; white subgroups show the largest 1985→1990 dollar gains but median declines in 1990→1996; only hispanic/female (+$9,101) shows a larger 1990→1996 dollar gain than black females' intervals.

## (3) Sensitivity check — black females with composite_wealth > 0 only
- 1985: n=813, median $4,800; 1990: n=978, median $11,057; 1996: n=956, median $25,050.
- 1985→1990: **+$6,257 (+130.4%)**; 1990→1996: **+$13,993 (+126.6%)**.
- **Stated caveat: excluding wealth ≤ 0 flips the largest-interval ranking to 1990→1996 in dollars**, so the robust full-sample conclusion (1985→1990) depends on retaining zero/negative net-worth respondents.

## (5) Workflow description (for payload)
Loaded `data/nls_incarceration_processed.csv` (12,013 rows, no missing values); filtered to race=='black' & sex=='female' (n=1,548); computed median composite wealth at 1985, 1990, 1996 and consecutive-wave changes in dollars (primary) and percent (secondary), retaining all respondents including zero/negative wealth; produced a race×sex subgroup context table for the same metrics; ran a sensitivity analysis restricted to composite_wealth>0; identified the largest interval (1985→1990 in the full sample; ranking flips under the positive-wealth restriction).

## Limitations
- datasets.json does not document which five NLS wealth variables compose each composite or whether definitions are identical across years — cross-year comparability is unverifiable.
- The 1985 black-female median ($175) sits in a large zero-wealth cluster, inflating percent change; dollar change is the primary metric for this reason.
- Extreme composite values (e.g., −$866,400 in 1990; +$4.06M) exist; medians are robust but distributional claims would not be.

**最终自然语言假设（含限定语）**：在 NLSY79 队列数据中，黑人女性（black females，n=1,548）的名义财富中位数增长最大的时期是 **1985 年至 1990 年**，其间中位数从约 $175 增至约 $2,600（净增约 $2,425，约 14 倍）；相比之下 1990–1996 年仅从约 $2,600 增至约 $4,000（净增约 $1,400，约 +54%），1985–1996 跨期累计净增约 $3,825。此结论基于名义美元、以绝对美元增量为口径、负值保留为净债务、无缺失（无需插补）、不使用权重与通胀调整；对极端值截断（p99）和将负值截为 0 的敏感性检验均不改变该排序。背景对比：黑人女性与其余五个 race×sex 组相比起点极低（1985 年中位数 $175 为全样本六组最低），1990 年代增幅放缓；白人两组的中位数在 1990 年见顶后在 1996 年回落，拉美裔两组则持续上升——说明黑人女性的"最大增长期"（1985–1990）与白人（1985–1990）一致、早于拉美裔（1990–1996）。

**证据（各表）**：
- 表1 黑人女性各年：1985 中位 $175（Q1=0, Q3=$5,000, n=1,548）；1990 中位 $2,600（Q1=0, Q3=$16,050）；1996 中位 $4,000（Q1=0, Q3=$42,512）。
- 表2 六组中位数与相邻年份增量（$）：
  | 组 | n | 1985 | 1990 | 1996 | Δ85–90 | Δ90–96 | Δ85–96 |
  | black_female | 1548 | 175 | 2600 | 4000 | **+2425** | +1400 | +3825 |
  | black_male | 1465 | 1400 | 3300 | 4200 | +1900 | +900 | +2800 |
  | hipanic_female | 986 | 2200 | 7649 | 16750 | +5449 | +9101 | +14550 |
  | hipanic_male | 915 | 4410 | 8400 | 14000 | +3990 | +5600 | +9590 |
  | white_female | 3630 | 5852.5 | 20100 | 8825 | +14247.5 | −11275 | +2972.5 |
  | white_male | 3469 | 5400 | 15601 | 8900 | +10201 | −6701 | +3500 |
  相对增长率（%）：black_female Δ85–90 约 +1,385.7%、Δ90–96 +53.8%；两种口径下 black_female 的最大增长期均为 1985–1990（相对口径下增幅比白人/黑人男性更极端，因其基数极低）。
- 稳健性（p99 截断，保留负值）：black female 三年截断后中位数与原值完全一致（175 / 2600 / 4000；p99 分别为 $130,107 / $261,335 / $413,550）——极端值不影响中位数结论。
- 敏感性（负值截为 0）：black female 三年中位数完全不变（175 / 2600 / 4000），因各年处于中位数以下的负值被置 0 后仍在分布下半部，不改变中位数位置；六组全部增量排序亦与主分析一致。即此前担心的"最大影响假设"实际对结果无影响，结论稳健。
- 数据完整性：三个 wealth 年份缺失值均为 0（race×sex 六组缺失率均为 0），故无插补/删除步骤；样本量三年相同（同批个体面板结构）。

**局限**：数据由 NLSY79 五个财富变量求和构成，无法核查变量清单与口径；race 取值 "hipanic" 疑为拼写错误，按原样处理；未做通胀调整，若按实际美元衡量，1985–1990 的增幅会相应缩小但排序（对 black female）不受影响，因为该判断只涉及同一组内两个相邻时期增量的相对大小（通胀按年份同比例作用于全样本，跨期比较中 1985–1990 与 1990–1996 的实际增量排序可能受通胀差异影响——1990–1996 年通胀更高，会进一步压低其实际增量，因此不会反转排序）。

ever_jailed is not needed to answer the headline question (it applies to 1985–1994 as a whole and cannot be attributed to a specific interval), but it will be summarized for subgroup context.

Composition of the 'five wealth variables' summed is undocumented, so component-level interpretation is not possible.
Bootstrap CIs on medians with ~30–40% zeros may be wide near the lower tail; conclusions rest primarily on point medians plus sensitivity checks.

ANALYSIS COMPLETE (result stage) — Wealth inequality among white males and white females, 1990 → 1996 (NLSY79 composite wealth, nominal USD)

Executed script: outputs/analysis_wealth_inequality.py (saved CSV outputs in outputs/). n = 3,469 white males, 3,630 white females; no missing values; negatives and zeros retained in the primary analysis.

== PRIMARY RESULTS (full distribution, negatives & zeros kept) ==

White males:
- Mean: $88,163 → $131,792 (+$43,630)
- Median: $15,601 → $8,900 (−$6,701)
- SD: $244,717 → $317,464 (+$72,747); CV: 2.776 → 2.409 (fell, because the mean rose proportionally faster than the SD)
- Gini: 0.781 → 0.794 (+0.012)
- P90/P50: 13.79 → 37.49 (nearly tripled)
- Top-decile (P90+) share: 0.621 → 0.620 (flat)
- P50/P10: undefined both years (P10 = $0; ~26%→43% of white males held exactly zero)

White females:
- Mean: $99,605 → $128,837 (+$29,232)
- Median: $20,100 → $8,825 (−$11,275)
- SD: $264,818 → $299,693 (+$34,875); CV: 2.659 → 2.326
- Gini: 0.763 → 0.778 (+0.015)
- P90/P50: 12.07 → 37.59 (nearly tripled)
- Top-decile share: 0.592 → 0.592 (flat)
- P50/P10: undefined both years (P10 = $0)

Cross-group levels (side-by-side, not the primary framing): females had a higher median than males in 1990 ($20,100 vs $15,601) but by 1996 both medians had converged to ~$8,800–8,900; Gini for females is slightly lower than males in both years.

== SENSITIVITY CHECKS ==
A) The single 1990 minimum outlier (−$866,400; it belongs to one white female) removed: all conclusions essentially unchanged (e.g., female 1990 Gini 0.7632→0.7626, mean $99,605→$99,871).
B) Top 1% winsorized per group-year: Gini still rises for both groups (males 0.763→0.784; females 0.733→0.769); top-decile share still ~flat-to-slightly-up; P90/P50 unchanged by construction. The upper-tail-driven inequality increase is robust.
C) Gini on positive wealth only: direction flips — Gini FALLS (males 0.689→0.623; females 0.681→0.599). This is the key instability: the rise in overall Gini comes from the growing mass at zero wealth, while dispersion among positive holders narrowed. So "inequality increased" is robust for top-vs-middle measures (P90/P50, winsorized Gini, SD) but not for positive-only Gini.

== DESCRIPTIVE ONLY: ever_jailed (small n, explicitly NOT part of the primary comparison) ==
Jailed white males n=57, jailed white females n=12. Jailed whites have far lower wealth (e.g., jailed white males: mean $26,066 in 1990, median $1,400; by 1996 median $0), versus never-jailed medians of $16,240/$9,450. Caveat stated in output: estimates unstable at these n, and ever_jailed (1985–1994) overlaps the 1990–1996 wealth window — no causal reading.

== ROBUST EMPIRICAL PATTERN (for the hypothesis synthesis) ==
Between 1990 and 1996, nominal mean wealth rose for both white males and white females while the median fell sharply; inequality as measured by top-vs-middle dispersion (P90/P50 roughly tripled in both groups) and Gini (modest rise) increased, with essentially no change in the top-decile share. The main driver appears to be a growing mass of respondents at zero wealth (zeros rose from ~26% to ~43% in both groups) combined with growing top values — i.e., polarization of the wealth distribution rather than a uniform spread. The result is robust to removing the 1990 outlier and to winsorizing the top 1%, but reverses under a positive-only Gini, which must be flagged.

== LIMITATIONS (to be stated in the final answer) ==
1. Composite wealth is assumed to be nominal US dollars (sum of five NLSY wealth items); no price index is in the data, so the 1990 vs 1996 comparison is nominal — real-dollar inequality could differ.
2. The exact construction of the five summed wealth components cannot be verified from the file alone.
3. Zero wealth (P10 = $0 in both waves) makes P50/P10 undefined and makes any inequality conclusion sensitive to how zeros are treated (full Gini rises, positive-only Gini falls).
4. ever_jailed findings are descriptive only (n=57/12) and cannot support causal claims.

Ready for your synthesis request for the natural-language hypothesis.

HYPOTHESIS: Between 1990 and 1996, wealth inequality increased within both white males and white females in the NLSY79 cohort, and the increase took the form of polarization rather than a uniform spreading of the distribution. In both groups, mean composite wealth rose (white males: $88,163 → $131,792; white females: $99,605 → $128,837, nominal) while the median fell sharply (males: $15,601 → $8,900; females: $20,100 → $8,825) and the share of respondents with exactly zero wealth grew from roughly 26% to roughly 43% in each group. The upper tail pulled away from the middle: the P90/P50 ratio nearly tripled (males 13.8 → 37.5; females 12.1 → 37.6) and the overall Gini rose modestly (males 0.781 → 0.794; females 0.763 → 0.778), while the top-decile wealth share stayed essentially flat (males ~0.62; females ~0.59). We therefore hypothesize that 1990–1996 wealth growth among whites accrued disproportionately to those already at the top, hollowing out the middle and accumulating a larger zero-wealth mass, so that top-versus-middle inequality rose for both sexes. This increase is robust on top-vs-middle measures — it survives removal of the single extreme 1990 outlier (−$866,400) and top-1% winsorization (Gini still rises: males 0.763 → 0.784; females 0.733 → 0.769). It is, however, sensitive to how zero and negative wealth are treated: on a positive-holders-only Gini the direction reverses (males 0.689 → 0.623; females 0.681 → 0.599), meaning dispersion among positive-wealth holders actually narrowed while the zero-wealth mass grew; the polarization claim, not a universal "Gini rose" claim, is the defensible one. Side-by-side levels: white females had the higher median in 1990 ($20,100 vs $15,601), but by 1996 the two groups' medians had converged to ~$8,800–8,900, with females' Gini remaining slightly lower than males' in both years. Incarceration (ever_jailed, descriptive only, small n: 57 jailed white males, 12 jailed white females) is associated with much lower wealth (jailed white males' median fell to $0 by 1996), but with n this small and a jailing window (1985–1994) overlapping the wealth window, this is a caveat, not part of the primary claim. Limitations: values are assumed to be nominal US dollars with no deflator available in the data, so no inflation adjustment was possible; the exact construction of the five-item composite wealth variable cannot be verified from the file alone; and P10 = $0 in both waves makes P50/P10 undefined.

WORKFLOW: (1) Inspected data/nls_incarceration_processed.csv: 12,013 rows × 6 columns, no missing values; race×sex counts white male 3,469 / white female 3,630; identified 614 negative and 2,975 zero wealth values in 1990 and 358 negative and 4,561 zeros in 1996, plus a single 1990 outlier of −866,400. In both groups, mean composite wealth rose (white males: $88,163 → $131,792; white females: $99,605 → $128,837, nominal) while the median fell sharply (males: $15,601 → $8,900; females: $20,100 → $8,825) and the share of respondents with exactly zero wealth grew from roughly 26% to roughly 43% in each group. The upper tail pulled away from the middle: the P90/P50 ratio nearly tripled (males 13.8 → 37.5; females 12.1 → 37.6) and the overall Gini rose modestly (males 0.781 → 0.794; females 0.763 → 0.778), while the top-decile wealth share stayed essentially flat (males ~0.62; females ~0.59). We therefore hypothesize that 1990–1996 wealth growth among whites accrued disproportionately to those already at the top, hollowing out the middle and accumulating a larger zero-wealth mass, so that top-versus-middle inequality rose for both sexes. This increase is robust on top-vs-middle measures — it survives removal of the single extreme 1990 outlier (−$866,400) and top-1% winsorization (Gini still rises: males 0.763 → 0.784; females 0.733 → 0.769). Limitations: values are assumed to be nominal US dollars with no deflator available in the data, so no inflation adjustment was possible; the exact construction of the five-item composite wealth variable cannot be verified from the file alone; and P10 = $0 in both waves makes P50/P10 undefined.

ОТЧЁТ ПО ОСМОТРУ data/nls_incarceration_processed.csv

1. Структура и типы
- Файл: 12 013 строк × 6 колонок; пропусков (NaN) нет ни в одной колонке.
- Колонки: race (str), sex (str), ever_jailed (int 0/1), composite_wealth_1985/1990/1996 (int64, но 1990/1996 содержат дробные значения в хвосте — при чтении сохраняются как числа; тип колонки int64 из-за целых мод, дробные хвосты присутствуют, см. квантили).
- ВАЖНО (факт из данных): race содержит опечатку 'hipanic' вместо 'hispanic' (986+915 = 1901 наблюдений). Для нашего вопроса (только white) это не мешает, но фиксирую.

2. Группы и валидность wealth (white only)
- white: 7 099 наблюдений (female 3 630, male 3 469).
- ever_jailed внутри white: female — 12 jailed / 3 618 не-jailed; male — 57 jailed / 3 412 не-jailed. jailed-подгруппы очень малы → любые выводы по ever_jailed будут крайне ненадёжными по мощности.
- Пропусков как NaN нет, поэтому «валидность» wealth зависит от трактовки нулей:
  • Ровно нулевые значения wealth: 1990 — 2 975 (24.7%), 1996 — 4 561 (38.0%); 1985 — 3 209.
  • Минимумы: 1990 → −866 400; 1996 → −403 001; максимумы: 1990 → 4 060 077; 1996 → 3 836 910. Отрицательные значения есть и правдоподобны (долги): в white-группе neg1990: female 179 / male 127; neg1996: female 69 / male 66. Экстремумы тяжёлые (до ±миллионов) → нужны робастные статистики/винсоризация.
  • Красный флаг: доля ровно-нулевого wealth у белых скачет с 22.9% (1990) до 42.9% (1996) — тогда как у black/hipanic доля нулей почти не меняется. Это сильный признак того, что в 1996 часть нулей — это пропуски/«не спрашивали», закодированные нулём (в NLSY79 в 1996 секция активов была изменена), а не истинный нулевой капитал.
- Panel attrition: ID-колонки в файле НЕТ, поэтому прямое отслеживание выбывания_panel невозможно. Косвенные индикаторы на white-выборке: строк, где 1990≠0, а 1996=0 — male 728, female 913 (это много и согласуется с гипотезой «нулевой = missing» в 1996); строк с 1990=0 и 1996≠0 — male 115, female 106. «Оба года ноль»: male 775, female 632.

3. ПРЕДЛОЖЕНИЕ по подходу (только предложение, не расчёт)
Вопрос «what changes occurred in wealth inequality between 1990 and 1996» предлагаю понимать как: изменение и уровня, и рассеяния распределения богатства у белых мужчин vs белых женщин, плюс изменение гендерного разрыва.
- Основная таблица по каждой группе (white-male, white-female), отдельно 1990 и 1996: mean, median, p25/p75, p90, доля отрицательных, доля нулей, Gini/размах межквартильный. Медианы и квантили — первичны (распределение крайне скошено, mean неустойчив к миллионным выбросам); mean приводить с винсоризацией (например, 1%/99%) для устойчивости.
- «Изменение» показывать тремя способами: (a) сдвиг медианы/среднего в уровнях и в %, (b) изменение дисперсии/неравенства (IQR, Gini, p90/p10), (c) изменение гендерного разрыва внутри белых (female − male по годам).
- ever_jailed: ДА, показать отдельной строкой/срезом (jailed vs не-jailed внутри каждой половой группы), но явно пометить, что jailed-группы по 12 и 57 наблюдений — это описательная иллюстрация, а не доказательство (риск смещения attrition сюда же добавляется). Основной ответ — без разбиения по jail.
- Проверка чувствительности к трактовке нулей-1996: базовый сценарий (0 = истинный ноль) и альтернативный (нулевые 1996 = missing, исключены) — если вывод меняется, это обязательно отразить в гипотезе.
- Уровень значимости: при желании — bootstrap-ДИ для медиан/разницы (непараметрически), без параметрических тестов нормальности.

4. Явные допущения и неопределённости
- «Изменение богатства» = изменение распределения (уровни + неравенство + гендерный разрыв) между 1990 и 1996, а не индивидуальный рост (парный рост без ID посчитать нельзя).
- Допущение: composite_wealth сопоставимы между 1990 и 1996 (одна и та же сумма пяти компонент) — это следует из описания датасета, но внутренне проверить нечем.
- Ключевая неопределённость: аномальный рост доли нулей в 1996 у белых (22.9%→42.9%) — истинный нулевой капитал или missing, закодированный нулём? Это главный риск смещения; заложен анализ чувствительности.
- Отсутствие ID → panel attrition не идентифицируем напрямую; косвенные признаки указывают на возможное выбывание/пропуски в 1996.
- Отрицательные значения трактуем как честный чистый капитал (долги) — не обрезаем, только винсоризируем хвосты для mean.
- ever_jailed — потенциально отвлекающий фактор для основного вопроса; используем как пояснительный срез с оговоркой о мощности (12/57 наблюдений) и confounding ( jailed коррелирует с полом: 57/3469 мужчин vs 12/3630 женщин среди белых).
- Опечатка 'hipanic' на white-анализ не влияет; упомяну в отчёте, исправлять не буду (не наша целевая группа).

Жду подтверждения плана (особенно: трактовка нулей-1996 и включение ever_jailed-среза) перед содержательными расчётами.

payload.answer:
ГИПОТЕЗА (data-grounded, ответ на вопрос «What changes occurred in the wealth inequality for white males and females between 1990 and 1996?»)

Between 1990 and 1996, wealth among white NLSY79 respondents grew strongly in the upper part of the distribution but its picture at the bottom is ambiguous because the share of exactly-zero wealth among whites doubled (22.9% → 42.9%; stable for black/Hispanic groups), suggesting 1996 zeros largely encode missing asset data rather than true zero wealth. Under the base scenario (zeros = true zero wealth), the median wealth of both white males (15 601 → 8 900) and white females (20 100 → 8 825) collapsed and the modest female advantage of 1990 (+4 499, bootstrap 95% CI [1 100, 7 600]) disappeared by 1996 (−75, CI [−4 800, 4 303]) — i.e., a convergence to parity driven by the bottom of the distribution. Under the sensitivity scenario (zeros = missing, excluded) and on the consistent panel (non-zero in both waves), the opposite bottom-half picture emerges: median wealth roughly tripled for both sexes (men 42 000 → 124 063; women 49 088 → 127 220) and inequality fell (Gini: men 0.715 → 0.639, women 0.714 → 0.616; p90/p10 fell from ~132/265 to ~70/92), while the female–male median gap narrowed from +7 088 (CI barely including 0) / +9 716 on the panel (CI [399, 17 500]) to +3 158 (CI spanning zero) — i.e., the gender gap in median wealth among whites narrowed to statistical insignificance, and women's winsorized mean advantage (+4 313) even reversed to a male mean advantage (−8 343). Hypothesis: between 1990 and 1996 white men and white women experienced comparable, strong wealth growth in the measurable (non-zero) range with declining inequality, and the female–male wealth gap among whites narrowed from a small but significant female median advantage to a statistically insignificant difference; whether the lowest quartile genuinely lost ground or simply dropped out of measurement cannot be resolved with these data, and any real "impoverishment of the bottom" claim should be withheld.

1. Loaded data/nls_incarceration_processed.csv (12 013 × 6, no NaNs; noted typo 'hipanic' in race — does not affect white-only analysis). Filtered race == white (7 099 obs: 3 630 female, 3 469 male).
2. Three scenarios, all with negatives retained: A base (0 = true zero), B sensitivity (0 = missing, excluded per wave), C consistent panel (non-zero in both waves; gap-change compared on identical samples within each scenario, per your instruction).
3. Per group×year: n, mean, winsorized mean (1%/99%), median (bootstrap 95% CI, B=2000, seed 202601), p10/p25/p75/p90, IQR, p90/p10, Gini (mean-absolute-difference formula, valid with negatives), shares of negative and zero values.
4. Gender gap (female − male) per year per scenario with bootstrap CI for the median gap.
5. ever_jailed: descriptive slice only (n = 57 jailed men, 12 jailed women — underpowered, confounded, not part of the main answer).
6. Outputs: artifacts/analysis.py (executed), artifacts/results_scenario_A/B/C.csv, artifacts/results.pkl.

- Scenario A: medians male 15 601→8 900, female 20 100→8 825; winsorized means rise (male 81 587→126 019; female 88 479→123 901); Gini ~0.78–0.80 both years/sexes; zero share male 25.7%→43.3%, female 20.3%→42.6%; median gap 1990 +4 499 CI [1 100; 7 600] → 1996 −75 CI [−4 800; 4 303].
- Scenario B: medians male 42 000→124 063, female 49 088→127 220; Gini male 0.715→0.639, female 0.714→0.616; p90/p10 male 131.6→70.1, female 264.6→91.9; median gap +7 088 (CI [−701; 14 951]) → +3 158 (CI [−8 701; 14 805]); mean gap +4 313 → −8 343.
- Scenario C (n=1 851 male, 1 979 female panel): medians 48 100→127 010 (male), 57 816→131 000 (female); Gini 0.703→0.633 / 0.702→0.610; gap +9 716 CI [399; 17 500] → +3 990 CI [−8 700; 16 000].
- ever_jailed slice: jailed respondents have far lower wealth (median 0–1 400 vs ~16–20 k for non-jailed in 1990) but n = 12/57 — descriptive only.

SCENARIO DIVERGENCE (honestly stated, per your instruction): вывод о «падении медианного богатства» существует ТОЛЬКО в сценарии A и полностью объясняется удвоением доли нулей в 1996 у белых (диагностический признак missing-кодировки: у black/Hispanic доля нулей стабильна, при белых 22.9%→42.9%). В сценариях B/C богатство растёт и неравенство снижается. Согласованное между сценариями ядро вывода: (i) верхняя часть распределения богатства у белых обоих полов заметно выросла; (ii) гендерный разрыв медиан внутри белых сократился и в 1996 статистически незначим; (iii) при исключении нулей Gini и p90/p10 снижаются у обоих полов. - Gini при отрицательных значениях трактовать осторожно (основной вывод о динамике дублируется p90/p10 и IQR).
- Winsorized mean устойчив к хвостам, но не к систематическому missing-кодированию нулей.
- ever_jailed-срез: мощность (12/57) и confounding (jailed коррелирует с полом) — только иллюстрация.

payload.answer:
Análisis ejecutado según el plan aprobado. Resultados y evidencia:

## Tabla por grupo-año (base: dólares corrientes, negativos conservados; blancos solamente)

| año | sexo | n | media | mediana | p75 | p90 | p90/p50 | Gini | media/mediana | % ceros | % negativos |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1990 | male | 3.469 | 88.163 | 15.601 | 91.400 | 215.149 | 13,8 | 0,792 | 5,65 | 25,7% | 3,7% |
| 1990 | female | 3.630 | 99.605 | 20.100 | 109.000 | 242.550 | 12,1 | 0,776 | 4,95 | 20,3% | 4,9% |
| 1996 | male | 3.469 | 131.792 | 8.900 | 148.055 | 333.640 | 37,5 | 0,797 | 14,81 | 43,3% | 1,9% |
| 1996 | female | 3.630 | 128.837 | 8.825 | 152.875 | 331.750 | 37,6 | 0,782 | 14,60 | 42,6% | 1,9% |

p50/p10 no es calculable en la base (p10 = 0 en ambos sexos y años, por la masa de ceros); se reporta p90/p50 como métrica principal y p50/p10 en la variante sin ceros.

## (i) Desigualdad DENTRO de cada grupo, 1990 → 1996
- p90/p50 se triplica: hombres 13,8 → 37,5; mujeres 12,1 → 37,6. La mediana cae ~43% en ambos sexos (hombres 15.601→8.900; mujeres 20.100→8.825) mientras p90 sube ~55% (215k→334k; 243k→332k): la parte inferior de la distribución se hunde y la superior crece.
- Gini casi sin cambio (hombres 0,792→0,797; mujeres 0,776→0,782): la desigualdad "total" medida por Gini es estable; el cambio se concentra en la masa inferior (ceros) y la cola superior.
- media/mediana se triplica (5,7→14,8 hombres; 5,0→14,6 mujeres); CV baja ligeramente (2,78→2,41; 2,66→2,33).

## (ii) Desigualdad ENTRE sexos
- Brecha relativa de mediana: en 1990 la mediana femenina era un 29% superior a la masculina (razón H/M = 0,776); en 1996 ambas medianas convergen casi a la paridad (razón H/M = 1,008). La brecha entre sexos desaparece — pero por convergencia hacia abajo (la mediana femenina cayó más: −56% vs −43%).
- En media, en 1990 las mujeres superaban a los hombres (99,6k vs 88,2k) y en 1996 quedan prácticamente iguales (128,8k vs 131,8k).

## Incertidumbre C: efecto del salto en la proporción de ceros (CUANTIFICADO)
La proporción de ceros sube de ~20–26% (1990) a ~42–43% (1996) en ambos sexos. Excluyendo los ceros, el patrón SE INVIERTE: p90/p50 baja de 6,27→3,96 (hombres) y 5,66→3,81 (mujeres); Gini baja de 0,715→0,639 (hombres) y 0,714→0,616 (mujeres); mediana sube fuertemente (42.000→124.063 hombres; 49.088→127.220 mujeres). Es decir: el "aumento de desigualdad" del análisis base (p90/p50 ×3) se debe casi por completo a la expansión del grupo de riqueza cero; entre quienes tienen riqueza distinta de cero, la desigualdad relativa DISMINUYE y la mediana crece. La hipótesis debe declarar esta dependencia.

## Sensibilidad (no cambia las conclusiones cualitativas de cada variante)
- Winsorización p1–p99 (dentro de grupo-año): Gini baja levemente (0,792→0,766 hombres 1990; 0,776→0,735 mujeres 1990; similar en 1996); p90/p50 y medianas idénticas (percentiles ≤p99 no afectados). Conclusión base inalterada.
- Exclusión de negativos: conclusiones idénticas en dirección (p90/p50 12,3→32,0 hombres; 10,3→32,6 mujeres; Gini estable ~0,75–0,79).
- Valor extremo documentado: la observación más negativa de 1990 es −866.400 (mujer blanca), seguida de −185.370 y −113.647; los máximos son 4.060.077 / 3.792.973 / 3.717.537. La winsorización neutraliza su influencia sin alterar conclusiones.

## Nota de inflación (solicitada)
Análisis base en dólares corrientes. Ajustar 1996 a dólares de 1990 (≈ ÷1,22, inflación acumulada ~22%) haría la caída real de medianas aún más profunda: mediana 1996 ≈ 7.295 (hombres) y 7.234 (mujeres) en dólares de 1990, frente a 15.601 y 20.100 en 1990. Las razones de percentiles (p90/p50) y el Gini son invariantes a la inflación (escala común dentro de cada año), por lo que las métricas de desigualdad relativa no cambian; solo los niveles y las brechas de mediana expresadas en dólares de un mismo año se verían afectadas (la brecha H/M de 1990, 0,776, es un ratio y tampoco cambia).

## Hipótesis (lenguaje natural, fundamentada solo en las cifras anteriores)
Entre 1990 y 1996, la desigualdad de riqueza entre hombres y mujeres blancos desapareció en la mediana (de una ventaja femenina del ~29% a la paridad, razón H/M de 0,776 a 1,008), pero esa convergencia ocurrió hacia abajo: la mediana cayó para ambos sexos (hombres −43%, mujeres −56%) mientras la media subía (~+49% y +29%) y el percentil 90 crecía ~55%, triplicando la razón p90/p50 en ambos grupos (≈12–14 → ≈37). En consecuencia, la desigualdad DENTRO de cada grupo aumentó marcadamente en su mitad inferior y en la brecha media-mediana (media/mediana de ~5 a ~15), aunque el Gini se mantuvo casi constante (~0,78–0,80). Este hallazgo depende críticamente del aparente salto en la proporción de personas con riqueza cero (de ~20–26% a ~42–43%), posible artefacto de codificación en 1996: excluyendo los ceros, la desigualdad relativa dentro de cada grupo disminuye (p90/p50 de ~6 a ~4; Gini de ~0,71 a ~0,62–0,64) y la mediana crece, de modo que la lectura "aumenta la desigualdad interna" es condicional a tratar los ceros de 1996 como riqueza genuina. Los resultados son robustos a la winsorización p1–p99 y a la exclusión de valores negativos (tratados como deudas netas válidas en la base; extremo documentado: −866.400).

Artefactos: analysis/wealth_inequality.py (script ejecutado, no vacío), analysis/output.txt (salida completa con base, entre-sexos, las tres sensibilidades y nota de inflación), analysis/summary_table.csv (tabla por grupo-año).

## 自然语言假设（直接回答问题）

**在 1990 至 1996 年间，白人男性和白人女性的财富不平等经历了"两极化"式的变化：组内总体不平等（基尼系数）基本未变，但分布底部塌陷、上部拉伸——中位数大幅下降、零财富人群比例近乎翻倍、而分布上部（P90、P99）名义值明显增长；同时，两性之间的财富差距发生了方向性逆转，1990 年白人女性的财富水平高于白人男性，到 1996 年这一女性优势消失，两性差距基本抹平。**

具体而言（名义值，未做通胀折算）：

**组内不平等（白人男性 / 白人女性，1990 → 1996）**
- 基尼系数：男性 0.792 → 0.798（+0.005，Bootstrap 95% CI [−0.017, +0.026]，不显著）；女性 0.775 → 0.782（+0.006，CI [−0.017, +0.028]，不显著）。总体不平等程度几乎不变，维持在极高水平（约 0.78–0.80）。
- 但不平等的"构成"变了：P90/P50 从男性 13.8 → 37.5、女性 12.1 → 37.6，上部拉伸约 2.7–3.1 倍；同时中位数从男性 15,601 美元降至 8,900（−43%）、女性 20,100 降至 8,825（−56%）；零财富占比从男性 25.7% → 43.3%、女性 20.3% → 42.6%。即变化集中在分布底部（大量白人男性和女性滑入零财富）与中上部（P75、P90 名义值上升约 60–62%）。
- 顶层份额几乎不变：Top10% 财富份额男性稳定在 0.62、女性稳定在 0.59，Top1% 份额甚至略降（约 0.22 → 0.18）。

**两性之间的差距（男 − 女）**
- 1990 年：女性中位数高出男性约 4,499 美元（20,100 vs 15,601），女性均值高出约 11,442 美元（男/女均值比 0.89）。
- 1996 年：中位数差距仅 +75 美元（8,900 vs 8,825，基本持平），均值差距转为男性高出约 2,956 美元（比值 1.02）。
- 因此两性之间的差距在 1990→1996 间被消除：白人女性此前相对白人男性的财富优势消失，两性分布趋同于同一种"中位数下移、底部归零、上尾增长"的形态。

**局限**：所有数值为名义值，未对 1990–1996 年通胀进行折算；通胀统一缩放不影响比值类指标（P90/P50、份额）和基尼的方向性结论，但中位数/均值的具体降幅为名义口径。

## 敏感性检验与零值不确定性的影响方向
1. **剔除 |财富|>300 万极端值**：所有结论方向不变、幅度几乎不变（如基尼：男 0.78→0.79，女 0.76→0.77；中位数与两性差距同向变化）。结论不依赖极值。
2. **Winsorize 1%/99%**：与原始口径完全一致（P90/P50 增长、中位数下降、两性差距消失的方向均不变），明确判断：**winsorize 口径与原始口径结论一致**。
3. **含零 vs 剔除零**：这是唯一改变量化结论口径的检验。剔除零值后，中位数大幅上升（男 42,000→124,063；女 49,088→127,220），基尼反而下降（男 0.72→0.64；女 0.71→0.62）。这印证了核心机制——**不平等变化主要由底部人群滑入零财富驱动**：若 1996 年 38% 的零值部分源于缺失被编码为 0（数据层面无法区分），则 1996 年真实中位数会被低估、零财富比例会被高估，"中位数下降"的幅度可能被夸大；但两性差距消失的方向在两种口径下均成立（剔除零值时男性均值差距同样由 −6,435 转为 +8,241）。最终假设中"底部塌陷"的表述因此比"中位数下降"更稳健。

## 执行的工作流程
1. 读取 data/nls_incarceration_processed.csv（12,013 行 × 6 列，无缺失值），核对 race/sex/ever_jailed 分布与三个财富变量的范围、零值、负值、极端值。
2. 筛选 race==white，按 sex（男 3,469 / 女 3,630）分组，对 1990、1996 两年的 composite_wealth 分别计算：均值、中位数、P1/P25/P50/P75/P90/P99、P90/P50、均值/中位数比、基尼系数（含负值口径及截负到 0 口径）、零值/负值占比、Top10% 与 Top1% 财富份额。
3. 计算两性之间的差距（男 − 女）：中位数差、均值差、均值比、基尼差。
4. 敏感性检验：剔除 |财富|>3,000,000、winsorize 1%/99%、剔除零值、截负到 0 四种口径下重算全部指标。
5. Bootstrap（1,000 次重抽）给出基尼的 95% CI 及 1996−1990 变化量的 CI，判断变化是否统计显著。

## 自然语言假设（直接回答问题）

**在 1990 至 1996 年间，白人男性和白人女性的财富不平等经历了"两极化"式的变化：组内总体不平等（基尼系数）基本未变，但分布底部塌陷、上部拉伸——中位数大幅下降、零财富人群比例近乎翻倍、而分布上部（P90、P99）名义值明显增长；同时，两性之间的财富差距发生了方向性逆转，1990 年白人女性的财富水平高于白人男性，到 1996 年这一女性优势消失，两性差距基本抹平。**

具体而言（名义值，未做通胀折算）：

**组内不平等（白人男性 / 白人女性，1990 → 1996）**
- 基尼系数：男性 0.792 → 0.798（+0.005，Bootstrap 95% CI [−0.017, +0.026]，不显著）；女性 0.775 → 0.782（+0.006，CI [−0.017, +0.028]，不显著）。总体不平等程度几乎不变，维持在极高水平（约 0.78–0.80）。
- 但不平等的"构成"变了：P90/P50 从男性 13.8 → 37.5、女性 12.1 → 37.6，上部拉伸约 2.7–3.1 倍；同时中位数从男性 15,601 美元降至 8,900（−43%）、女性 20,100 降至 8,825（−56%）；零财富占比从男性 25.7% → 43.3%、女性 20.3% → 42.6%。即变化集中在分布底部（大量白人男性和女性滑入零财富）与中上部（P75、P90 名义值上升约 60–62%）。
- 顶层份额几乎不变：Top10% 财富份额男性稳定在 0.62、女性稳定在 0.59，Top1% 份额甚至略降（约 0.22 → 0.18）。

**两性之间的差距（男 − 女）**
- 1990 年：女性中位数高出男性约 4,499 美元（20,100 vs 15,601），女性均值高出约 11,442 美元（男/女均值比 0.89）。
- 1996 年：中位数差距仅 +75 美元（8,900 vs 8,825，基本持平），均值差距转为男性高出约 2,956 美元（比值 1.02）。
- 因此两性之间的差距在 1990→1996 间被消除：白人女性此前相对白人男性的财富优势消失，两性分布趋同于同一种"中位数下移、底部归零、上尾增长"的形态。

**局限**：所有数值为名义值，未对 1990–1996 年通胀进行折算；通胀统一缩放不影响比值类指标（P90/P50、份额）和基尼的方向性结论，但中位数/均值的具体降幅为名义口径。

## 敏感性检验与零值不确定性的影响方向
1. **剔除 |财富|>300 万极端值**：所有结论方向不变、幅度几乎不变（如基尼：男 0.78→0.79，女 0.76→0.77；中位数与两性差距同向变化）。结论不依赖极值。
2. **Winsorize 1%/99%**：与原始口径完全一致（P90/P50 增长、中位数下降、两性差距消失的方向均不变），明确判断：**winsorize 口径与原始口径结论一致**。
3. **含零 vs 剔除零**：这是唯一改变量化结论口径的检验。剔除零值后，中位数大幅上升（男 42,000→124,063；女 49,088→127,220），基尼反而下降（男 0.72→0.64；女 0.71→0.62）。这印证了核心机制——**不平等变化主要由底部人群滑入零财富驱动**：若 1996 年 38% 的零值部分源于缺失被编码为 0（数据层面无法区分），则 1996 年真实中位数会被低估、零财富比例会被高估，"中位数下降"的幅度可能被夸大；但两性差距消失的方向在两种口径下均成立（剔除零值时男性均值差距同样由 −6,435 转为 +8,241）。最终假设中"底部塌陷"的表述因此比"中位数下降"更稳健。

- **Negatives:** 649 (1985), 614 (1990), 358 (1996) negative values overall. White males: 161/127/66; white females: 209/179/69. (Plausible real net-worth negatives, but could also indicate coding issues — e.g., −$866,400 in 1990 looks like a possible data-entry/coding outlier.)

## 2. Proposed analytical approach

For white males and white females separately, compute for 1990 and 1996 (with 1985 as optional context):
1. **Location/spread:** mean, median, SD, coefficient of variation, and selected quantiles (p10, p25, p75, p90).
2. **Inequality/dispersion measures:**

   - **Top-tail concentration:** top 10% / top 1% wealth shares.

3. **Composition shifts:** share with zero wealth, share negative, share positive — this turns out to be a first-order driver of the 1990→1996 change (zero share roughly doubles).
4. **Sex comparison over time:** Δ (1996 − 1990) in each measure for males vs. females, plus a change-in-change comparison; optionally a bootstrap (e.g., 1,000 resamples) for uncertainty on the Gini/CV changes.
5. **Sensitivity checks:** (a) with vs. without exact duplicate rows; (b) with vs. without the extreme negative 1990 outlier; (c) Gini including vs. excluding negatives.

The zero-wealth share roughly doubled (white males 25.7%→43.3%; white females 20.3%→42.6%), the median wealth **fell** (males $15,601→$8,900; females $20,100→$8,825), while mean wealth and the 90th percentile **rose** (males: mean $88,163→$131,792, p90 $215k→$334k; females: mean $99,605→$128,837, p90 $243k→$332k) — i.e., wealth became **more polarized** (a swelling zero-wealth bottom and a richer top), yet **relative dispersion among the wealthy narrowed** (p90/p10 among positive-wealth holders: males 68.2→51.1; females 84.0→55.3; Gini on positives: males 0.688→0.623; females 0.681→0.599; CV: males 2.78→2.41; females 2.66→2.33). By contrast, the **Gini over the full distribution (negatives included) barely moved** (males 0.792→0.797; females 0.776→0.782) because the growing zero-wealth mass offsets the compression above zero. The female pattern was slightly stronger than the male pattern: females had a larger drop in positive-only Gini (Δ −0.082 vs −0.066) and a larger rise in the zero share (+22.2pp vs +17.7pp), whereas males gained more mean wealth (+$43.6k vs +$29.2k) and their top-1% share fell less. Net: **inequality "compressed" in relative terms for both sexes — somewhat more for females — while the distribution itself became more bimodal (zero-wealth bottom vs. richer top) for both sexes.**

|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|

## (b) Male-vs-female change-in-change (Δ = 1996 − 1990)

| measure | male Δ | female Δ | ΔΔ (male − female) |
|---|---|---|---|
| CV | −0.367 | −0.333 | −0.034 |
| Gini (all, negatives incl.) | +0.005 | +0.006 | −0.001 |

| median | −$6,701 | −$11,275 | +$4,574 |

| negative share | −1.8pp | −3.0pp | +1.3pp |
| p90 | +$118,491 | +$89,200 | +$29,291 |

## (c) Bootstrap uncertainty (1,000 paired resamples, 95% CI)

- **White male:** ΔCV = −0.359 [−0.623, −0.079]; ΔGini(pos) = −0.066 [−0.090, −0.041] (significant); ΔGini(all) = +0.006 [−0.010, +0.023] (not significant); Δp90/p50 = +26.3 [+14.5, +43.8] (significant increase — upper tail stretches relative to a shrinking median).

## (e) Workflow description (for submission)

Loaded `nls_incarceration_processed.csv` (12,013 rows, no NaNs; white males n=3,469, white females n=3,630). For each sex × year (1990, 1996), computed mean, median, SD, CV, p10/p25/p50/p75/p90, p90/p10 (positives), p90/p50, p75/p25, Gini via the O(n log n) sorted-rank formula on the full distribution (negatives included) and on positives only, top-10%/top-1% positive-wealth shares, and zero/negative/positive shares; then within-sex 1990→1996 changes and the male-vs-female change-in-change, with 1,000-resample paired bootstrap CIs on the dispersion changes (seed 20261019). ## Caveats carried into the answer

1. **Zeros-as-missing:** zeros are treated as true zero wealth by default; if they encode NLS missing codes, the doubling of the zero share (and the median decline) could partly reflect item-nonresponse growth rather than real impoverishment — though the exclude-zeros sensitivity shows the same relative-inequality decline among holders of positive wealth.
2. **No panel tracking:** the file has no person ID, so 1990 and 1996 are compared as repeated cross-sections; within-person wealth mobility cannot be measured.
3. **Attrition:** NLSY79 1979-cohort attrition between waves cannot be assessed or corrected here; if wealth-selective, it could bias the wave comparison.
4. **Duplicates:** 1,899 exact duplicate rows (overwhelmingly all-zero wealth) are retained in the primary run per the approved plan; the deduplicated run is reported alongside.
5. Gini on a distribution containing negatives is reported but interpreted with care (the positives-only Gini and CV are the more robust dispersion indicators here).

FULL ANALYSIS EXECUTED — SYNTHESIS-READY RESULTS

NATURAL-LANGUAGE HYPOTHESIS (final answer draft):
"Across the NLSY79 cohort (N = 12,013; 289 individuals jailed at some point during 1985–1994), individuals with a criminal record had significantly lower wealth than those without a record in ALL THREE years examined — 1985, 1990, and 1996 (all p < 0.001 on Welch t-tests and Mann–Whitney U tests, and all p < 0.05 in race/sex-adjusted robust regressions). The wealth gap widened over time: jailed individuals averaged ~$7,929 vs ~$25,086 in 1985 (mean difference ≈ −$17,157), ~$16,350 vs ~$73,948 in 1990 (≈ −$57,598), and ~$20,383 vs ~$105,447 in 1996 (≈ −$85,064), with medians of $720 vs $3,600 (1985), $0 vs $10,500 (1990), and $0 vs $8,500 (1996). Importantly, the timing frame changes the interpretation: because ever_jailed covers only 1985–1994, the significant 1985 gap is best read as a PRE-EXISTING (pre-incarceration/selection) difference rather than an effect of incarceration, whereas the significant 1990 and 1996 gaps — especially the much larger 1996 gap — are consistent with wealth divergence during and after the incarceration window. The data show association, not causation."

WHICH YEARS ARE "SIGNIFICANTLY LOWER": ALL THREE (1985, 1990, 1996), with NO test disagreement anywhere — Welch t-test, one-sided Mann–Whitney (H1: jailed < not-jailed), winsorized t-test, HC3-adjusted OLS, and median (quantile) regression all reject at α = 0.05 in every year.

KEY NUMBERS (unadjusted, jailed n=289 vs not-jailed n=11,724):
- 1985: Welch t = −9.78, p = 6.3e−21; MWU p(one-sided less) = 8.0e−11 (two-sided 1.6e−10); mean diff −17,157
- 1990: Welch t = −9.57, p = 1.6e−19; MWU p(less) = 3.9e−35 (two-sided 7.8e−35); mean diff −57,598
- 1996: Welch t = −9.72, p = 7.3e−20; MWU p(less) = 4.6e−26 (two-sided 9.3e−26); mean diff −85,064

ADJUSTED (race + sex, HC3-robust OLS), ever_jailed coefficient:
- 1985: −9,441 (95% CI [−13,043, −5,839]), p = 2.8e−07
- 1990: −35,394 (95% CI [−47,796, −22,992]), p = 2.2e−08
- 1996: −60,911 (95% CI [−78,761, −43,061]), p = 2.3e−11
Median (quantile) regression coefficients (adjusted): −1,100 (p=0.021), −3,800 (p=0.016), −6,000 (p=0.0003) — smaller because medians sit near zero for the jailed group, but all still significant at 0.05.
Sensitivity: winsorized (1%/99%) Welch t-tests: p = 9.3e−16 / 8.8e−27 / 7.7e−35 for 1985/1990/1996 — conclusions robust to outliers.

METHODOLOGY NOTES HONORING THE APPROVED PLAN:
- Negatives retained as-is (net worth interpretation); original data values were never modified — 'hipanic' handled only via label mapping in the model formula, and no altered dataset was saved (artifacts are the script plus two output CSVs of results).

- R² of adjusted models is small (0.009–0.019): ever_jailed, race and sex explain little wealth variance overall — the gap is significant but wealth is dominated by other (unobserved) factors.

TIMING NUANCE (explicitly in the hypothesis wording, per your instruction): "found to have significantly lower wealth" is reported as association in all three years, with 1985 interpreted as a pre-existing gap (pre-incarceration), 1990 as mixed during-window, and 1996 as post-incarceration. No causal claim.

LIMITATIONS / UNCERTAINTIES:
1. Units/scale of composite wealth undocumented (assumed USD); exact composition of the "five wealth variables" unknown.
2. ever_jailed misses arrests without jail; "criminal record" is operationalized narrowly.
3. No survey weights or attrition correction available in the processed file.
4. Heavy right skew (6.5–16.8) and ~3–5% zeros/negatives — hence the dual-test approach; MWU and t-test agree everywhere, so no interpretive conflict to report.
5. Adjusted models control only for race and sex; residual confounding (education, family background, prior wealth) is unaddressed, reinforcing the non-causal framing.

СТАТИСТИКА ОСМОТРА:
• ever_jailed: 289 из 12013 (2.4%) сидели; сильный дисбаланс групп (1:40), все выводы будут держаться в основном на ~289 наблюдениях.

• Wealth (все три года): сильный правый перекос (skew 6.5–16.8, эксцесс 59–372), длинный хвост до $2.6M–4M. Отрицательные значения есть и вездесущи: 649/614/358 наблюдений <0 (минимумы −57.6k / −866k / −403k) — это чистый долг (композит = сумма активов; отрицательные = обязательства превышают активы).
